Appendix.title: Automatic differentiation and backpropagation
Appendix.Content: Automatic differentiation and backpropagation
Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: University courses · Latest development: Phase 9
Definition and mechanism

Automatic differentiation evaluates derivatives by applying the chain rule to the operations in a program. Each operation has a local derivative rule; composing the rules gives the derivative of the complete computation without symbolically expanding it or approximating it by finite differences. Forward mode propagates a tangent perturbation and computes a Jacobian-vector product (JVP), useful when there are few inputs. Reverse mode propagates sensitivities from outputs back to inputs and computes a vector-Jacobian product (VJP), making gradients of one scalar loss with respect to millions of parameters practical. Backpropagation is reverse-mode differentiation through a neural network’s computation graph. It does not remove numerical problems: nondifferentiable operations require conventions, saturated activations can yield tiny gradients, and an incorrect graph or reduction yields an incorrect gradient. Gradients are local sensitivity information, not proof of a global optimum. Finite differences remain a useful small-scale check, but cancellation and step-size tradeoffs make them a poor training method.
Phase 9–10 development

Forward mode propagates an input tangent through local derivatives and computes a Jacobian-vector product. Reverse mode propagates an output sensitivity backward and computes a vector-Jacobian product. These are chain-rule evaluations on the operation graph, distinct from finite differences, which perturb inputs and can suffer cancellation. The reverse pass requires a valid reverse-topological order and storage that remains alive until propagation finishes. Differentiating a converged solution uses an implicit equation and its local Jacobian; it is not automatically the same as differentiating every solver iteration.

Appendix.title: Continuous collision detection
Appendix.Content: Continuous collision detection

Discrete collision detection tests shapes at selected instants. If an object moves from one side of a thin obstacle to the other between two simulation states, both endpoint tests can be non-overlapping even though the swept motion intersects. Continuous collision detection asks about the whole interval.
A CCD result is only meaningful after the motion model is stated: constant linear velocity, linear interpolation of transforms, rigid rotation, acceleration bound, deforming vertices, and so on.
Time of impact
For simple primitives, time of impact can sometimes be solved analytically. For example, sphere-sphere CCD under constant relative velocity reduces to a quadratic in time.

For general convex shapes, conservative advancement repeatedly estimates separation distance <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>d</mi> </math> and an upper bound on closing speed <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <msub> <mi>v</mi> <mi>c</mi> </msub> </math>, then advances by a safe amount related to
Appendix.RawBlock: <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block"> <mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi> <mi>t</mi> <mo>≤</mo> <mfrac> <mi>d</mi> <msub> <mi>v</mi> <mi>c</mi> </msub> </mfrac> <mo>.</mo> </math>
Appendix.Content: The bound must account for all motion capable of reducing separation. Using only translational relative speed can be unsafe for rotating shapes whose extremal points sweep quickly.
Conservative versus exact

A conservative CCD algorithm may report contact slightly early but should not step past a true collision under its assumptions. Early contact changes simulation, so conservatism still has a measurable quality cost.
Iteration limits need an explicit outcome: separated, hit, no convergence/uncertain. Returning “no collision” when the solver simply exhausted iterations turns a performance cap into tunneling.
Robustness

Near tangency, distance and time estimates become sensitive. Scale-aware tolerances should relate to object size, velocity/time scale and numerical precision. A single global epsilon is rarely correct.
Initial overlap is also a separate case: TOI = 0 may be meaningful, but penetration recovery and contact normal are not automatically solved by a sweep routine.
Verification

Differential tests can compare an optimized CCD against dense time sampling for cases where dense sampling is a reliable conservative oracle, plus analytic primitive cases. Property tests should vary scale, velocity, near-tangent trajectories and iteration limits.
The repository already contains disk CCD/swept broadphase witnesses; those are not proof of arbitrary rotating convex CCD.
Read the connected explanation in Continuous Notes/University - Worlds, Images and Inference - Graphics, Vision and Photography#From a Scene to a Collision Answer: Geometry as a Chain of Contracts.

Appendix.title: Convolution and filter footprints
Appendix.Content: Convolution and filter footprints
Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: XR01 · Latest development: University courses
Definition and mechanism

Convolution combines shifted values with a weighting kernel; its spectrum multiplies transfer functions. Pixel footprints and boundary policies define what is averaged. A separable Gaussian uses two 1D passes; unpadded DFT filtering wraps circularly.
Prerequisites

ListItem.Content: Continuous signals and discrete samples — Filtering/frequency analysis operates on a declared domain and its samples.
Fourier analysis and spectral phase — Frequency and phase reveal transfer, sampling ambiguity and structural loss.

Appendix.Content: Used by

Content.Link: Optical flow and time to contact

ListItem.Content: Learned image features and CNNs ## Recall and next depth

Appendix.Content: Derive the three-tap filter’s gain and constant preservation. Pending: implementation cost, padding and spatially varying kernels. Written coverage is not a claim of learner mastery or accepted numbered-curriculum progress.
Source and navigation
Expanded teaching explanation · Independent coverage · Dependency Map
University course development

Extend the current convolution note from a sliding kernel to image formation and resampling. A pixel integrates incoming image energy over a finite footprint; point sampling is only an approximation to that area integral. Convolution combines nearby values with weights whose spatial support is the kernel footprint, and its Fourier transform describes which spatial frequencies survive. Before reducing resolution, low-pass filtering suppresses frequencies the coarser grid cannot represent. In texture mapping, the screen-to-texture Jacobian maps a nearly square screen pixel to a texture-space parallelogram. If the two singular directions have very different lengths, an isotropic mip level blurs one direction too much; anisotropic filters take extra samples along the long axis. This same footprint reasoning links pixel reconstruction, antialiasing, texture filtering, and sensor blur without treating them as unrelated tricks.
Sampling continuous signals and image formation · Image sampling, filtering, and efficient reconstruction · Textures and surface detail

Appendix.title: Depth buffering and visibility order
Appendix.Content: Depth buffering and visibility order
Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: University courses · Latest development: University courses
Definition and mechanism

A depth buffer stores the nearest depth seen so far for each image sample. When rasterizing a fragment, compare its depth with the stored value; if it is closer, update both depth and color, otherwise discard it. This per-sample test resolves opaque visibility without sorting all triangles. Perspective projection maps view-space depth nonlinearly, so the near and far clipping planes affect how floating-point precision is distributed. If they span an unnecessarily huge ratio, nearly coplanar surfaces may quantize to equal or inconsistent depths and flicker as the camera moves; this is z-fighting. Alpha-blended surfaces need additional ordering or order-independent methods because color composition is not commutative. Depth establishes visibility, while transparency determines how multiple visible layers contribute.
Prerequisites
Used by

ListItem.Content: Hardware depth-buffer linearization ## Full teaching explanation

Appendix.Content: Rasterization, coverage, and depth · Textures and surface detail
Phase 11 camera development

Depth gives ordering or camera-relative distance under a specific projection convention; it does not identify the surface that produced a sample. Reprojecting old color and depth can place history behind a newly visible surface. Validate with current depth, normal, object identity, or neighborhood checks; reject disocclusions and large reprojection errors. Reversed-Z and nonlinear perspective depth require consistent reconstruction before threshold comparisons. Valid visibility does not guarantee photometric stability after lighting, exposure, or material changes. Link depth semantics to temporal history validation. Link: A camera model must close the loop; research: Four deeper links from the TUM lecture review.

Appendix.title: Dual quaternion skinning
Appendix.Content: Dual quaternion skinning

Linear blend skinning blends transformed vertex positions or bone matrices. It is simple and GPU-friendly, but blending rotation matrices componentwise is not itself a rigid transformation and can collapse volume around twisting joints.
Dual quaternions provide a representation of rigid motion that blends rotation and translation together before transforming the point.
A dual quaternion is
Appendix.RawBlock: <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block"> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"> <mover> <mi>q</mi> <mo stretchy="false">^</mo> </mover> </mrow> <mo>=</mo> <msub> <mi>q</mi> <mi>r</mi> </msub> <mo>+</mo> <mi>ε</mi> <msub> <mi>q</mi> <mi>d</mi> </msub> <mo>,</mo> <mstyle scriptlevel="0"> <mspace width="2em" /> </mstyle> <msup> <mi>ε</mi> <mn>2</mn> </msup> <mo>=</mo> <mn>0</mn> <mo>,</mo> </math>
Appendix.Content: where <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <msub> <mi>q</mi> <mi>r</mi> </msub> </math> is a unit rotation quaternion. For translation vector <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>t</mi> </math> represented as pure quaternion <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <msub> <mi>t</mi> <mi>q</mi> </msub> <mo>=</mo> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mn>0</mn> <mo>,</mo> <mi>t</mi> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </math> under one common convention,
Appendix.RawBlock: <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block"> <msub> <mi>q</mi> <mi>d</mi> </msub> <mo>=</mo> <mfrac> <mn>1</mn> <mn>2</mn> </mfrac> <msub> <mi>t</mi> <mi>q</mi> </msub> <msub> <mi>q</mi> <mi>r</mi> </msub> <mo>.</mo> </math>
Appendix.Content: The translation can be recovered by
Appendix.RawBlock: <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block"> <msub> <mi>t</mi> <mi>q</mi> </msub> <mo>=</mo> <mn>2</mn> <msub> <mi>q</mi> <mi>d</mi> </msub> <msubsup> <mi>q</mi> <mi>r</mi> <mo>∗</mo> </msubsup> <mo>.</mo> </math>
Appendix.Content: Antipodal problem

Rotation quaternions <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>q</mi> </math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mo>−</mo> <mi>q</mi> </math> encode the same physical rotation. Their corresponding dual quaternions likewise differ by a global sign. If two equivalent bones/poses are blended without hemisphere alignment, their real parts can cancel.
Before weighted blending, choose a reference real quaternion and flip any dual quaternion whose real part has negative dot product with that reference.
After blending,
Appendix.RawBlock: <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block"> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"> <mover> <mi>q</mi> <mo stretchy="false">^</mo> </mover> </mrow> <mo>=</mo> <munder> <mo data-mjx-texclass="OP">∑</mo> <mi>i</mi> </munder> <msub> <mi>w</mi> <mi>i</mi> </msub> <msub> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"> <mover> <mi>q</mi> <mo stretchy="false">^</mo> </mover> </mrow> <mi>i</mi> </msub> <mo>,</mo> </math>
Appendix.Content: normalize the real quaternion magnitude and apply the same scale to the dual part. This is normalized dual-quaternion blending. It represents rigid blending; ordinary dual-quaternion skinning does not directly encode arbitrary nonuniform scale or shear.
Bind transforms
Skinning still needs the same coordinate contract as matrix skinning:
current bone world transform × inverse bind transform
must produce the deformation from bind-space vertex to current posed space. Dual quaternions change the representation/blending mechanism, not the ownership of coordinate spaces.
Executable witness

tools/labs/dual_quaternion_skinning_lab.cpp constructs rigid transforms from quaternion + translation, transforms points, checks distance preservation, blends pure translations, and deliberately blends a dual quaternion with its globally negated equivalent to prove antipodal alignment prevents cancellation.
It does not yet prove arbitrary multi-joint skinning, scale/shear, GPU implementation, inverse-bind import or production animation parity.
Related: Quaternion rotation and double cover, Quaternion interpolation and shortest paths, Transform hierarchies TRS and shear.

Appendix.title: Exposure and sensor response
Appendix.Content: Exposure and sensor response
Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: University courses · Latest development: University courses
Definition and mechanism

A camera sensor converts arriving photons into electrical measurements. Exposure depends on scene radiance, lens transmission, aperture, shutter duration, and sensor sensitivity; changing these settings trades motion blur, depth of field, noise, and saturation. A pixel integrates light over a finite area and exposure interval before quantization. Sensor wells have finite capacity, so highlights clip, while low photon counts have shot noise and readout adds electronic noise. ISO gain amplifies the signal and its noise rather than collecting additional photons. The recorded raw values are not yet display colors: white balance, color transforms, tone curves, and transfer encoding turn measurements into an image. A camera model must distinguish photon capture, sensor response, and display rendering to explain dynamic range and exposure choices.
Prerequisites

Appendix.title: GJK and EPA
Appendix.Content: GJK and EPA
GJK answers geometric questions about two convex shapes by working with their Minkowski difference
Appendix.RawBlock: <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block"> <mi>A</mi> <mo>−</mo> <mi>B</mi> <mo>=</mo> <mo fence="false" stretchy="false">{</mo> <mi>a</mi> <mo>−</mo> <mi>b</mi> <mo>∣</mo> <mi>a</mi> <mo>∈</mo> <mi>A</mi> <mo>,</mo> <mi>b</mi> <mo>∈</mo> <mi>B</mi> <mo fence="false" stretchy="false">}</mo> <mo>.</mo> </math>
Appendix.Content: The shapes intersect exactly when the origin lies inside <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>A</mi> <mo>−</mo> <mi>B</mi> </math>. The algorithm does not construct that difference explicitly. It asks each shape for an extreme support point. For search direction <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>d</mi> </math>,
Appendix.RawBlock: <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block"> <mi>s</mi> <mi>u</mi> <mi>p</mi> <mi>p</mi> <mi>o</mi> <mi>r</mi> <msub> <mi>t</mi> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"> <mi>A</mi> <mo>−</mo> <mi>B</mi> </mrow> </msub> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mi>d</mi> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> <mo>=</mo> <mi>s</mi> <mi>u</mi> <mi>p</mi> <mi>p</mi> <mi>o</mi> <mi>r</mi> <msub> <mi>t</mi> <mi>A</mi> </msub> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mi>d</mi> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> <mo>−</mo> <mi>s</mi> <mi>u</mi> <mi>p</mi> <mi>p</mi> <mi>o</mi> <mi>r</mi> <msub> <mi>t</mi> <mi>B</mi> </msub> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mo>−</mo> <mi>d</mi> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> <mo>.</mo> </math>
Appendix.Content: Each support query adds one point, and GJK maintains a simplex containing at most four support points in 3D.
Simplex evolution

A simplex may be a point, segment, triangle or tetrahedron. The update step determines which Voronoi region of the simplex can still contain the closest point to the origin, discards vertices that cannot matter, and produces a new search direction.
This geometric classification is the heart of GJK. Memorizing a chain of cross products without the region argument makes degeneracy bugs almost impossible to diagnose.
A production implementation must define behavior for repeated support points, nearly collinear segments, nearly coplanar triangles, tiny search directions and finite iteration limits.

Intersection-GJK and distance-GJK use related simplexes but do not have identical termination rules. A condition sufficient to say “origin cannot be passed in this direction” is not automatically a high-quality distance convergence test.
Termination and finite precision

Exact zero comparisons are brittle. Useful termination signals include lack of support progress, lack of distance improvement, repeated support points, simplex containment within tolerance, and an explicit maximum iteration count.
Every exit should identify the reason. An iteration cap is “uncertain/no convergence” unless the algorithm has another conservative proof of separation or intersection.
EPA after intersection
When GJK produces an appropriate simplex/polytope enclosing the origin, EPA estimates penetration by refining the boundary of that Minkowski polytope.
The core loop is:

ListItem.Content: find the face closest to the origin;
query a support point in the outward face normal;
compare the new support distance with the current face distance;
if their gap is within tolerance, return the face normal/depth approximation;
otherwise remove faces visible from the new support point;
extract the horizon boundary;
connect the new point to the horizon and continue.

Appendix.Content: EPA therefore owns topology as well as geometry. Incorrect face orientation or horizon ordering can create an inside-out polytope even when GJK was correct.
Finite support-gap tolerance gives an approximation. EPA should not be described as exact penetration recovery for arbitrary floating-point convex shapes.
Contact generation is later

A penetration normal and depth are not a persistent contact manifold. The physics engine still needs witness/contact points, feature identity, clipping or support-feature reconstruction, warm-start keys, friction basis and lifetime policy.
Read the connected explanation in Continuous Notes/University - Worlds, Images and Inference - Graphics, Vision and Photography#From a Scene to a Collision Answer: Geometry as a Chain of Contracts.
Related: Continuous collision detection, Minkowski sums and support mappings, Persistent contact manifolds.

Appendix.title: Half-edge mesh connectivity
Appendix.Content: Half-edge mesh connectivity
Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: University courses · Latest development: University courses
Definition and mechanism

A half-edge data structure stores each undirected edge as two opposite directed records. Each record points to its twin, the next directed edge around its face, its origin vertex, its edge, and its face; vertices, edges, and faces keep one representative half-edge. Repeatedly following next visits a face boundary. Following twin then next walks around a vertex fan. This makes local neighborhoods and edits proportional to local degree rather than requiring a scan of every face. Correctness depends on invariants: twin of twin returns to the original, a half-edge is not its own twin, and next pointers form closed face cycles. The representation naturally assumes manifold connectivity; it can encode flips, splits, and collapses by changing a bounded set of pointers, but careless updates can break the cycles and corrupt subsequent traversal.
Prerequisites

Content.Link: Manifold polygon meshes and boundary structure

Appendix.Content: Used by

ListItem.Content: Local rigidity and mesh orientation fields ## Full teaching explanation

Appendix.title: Half-edge topology invariants
Appendix.Content: Half-edge topology invariants

A triangle index buffer tells the renderer which three vertices form each face, but many geometry-processing algorithms need explicit adjacency: which face lies across an edge, which edges surround a vertex, and where the mesh boundary is.

A half-edge representation splits every undirected edge into directed records attached to faces. For triangle face <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <msub> <mi>v</mi> <mn>0</mn> </msub> <mo>,</mo> <msub> <mi>v</mi> <mn>1</mn> </msub> <mo>,</mo> <msub> <mi>v</mi> <mn>2</mn> </msub> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </math>, create directed half-edges
Appendix.RawBlock: <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block"> <msub> <mi>v</mi> <mn>0</mn> </msub> <mo stretchy="false">→</mo> <msub> <mi>v</mi> <mn>1</mn> </msub> <mo>,</mo> <mstyle scriptlevel="0"> <mspace width="1em" /> </mstyle> <msub> <mi>v</mi> <mn>1</mn> </msub> <mo stretchy="false">→</mo> <msub> <mi>v</mi> <mn>2</mn> </msub> <mo>,</mo> <mstyle scriptlevel="0"> <mspace width="1em" /> </mstyle> <msub> <mi>v</mi> <mn>2</mn> </msub> <mo stretchy="false">→</mo> <msub> <mi>v</mi> <mn>0</mn> </msub> <mo>.</mo> </math>
Appendix.Content: For a consistently oriented two-manifold interior edge, exactly two half-edges share the same undirected endpoints and they run in opposite directions. They become twins.
Invariants
A useful topology builder should establish:

ListItem.Content: every face vertex index is valid;
a face does not repeat one of its own vertices;
each directed edge appears at most once for an oriented manifold triangle mesh;
an undirected edge with one incident face is a boundary edge;
an undirected edge with two incident faces is manifold only when directions oppose;
an undirected edge with more than two incident faces is non-manifold;
twin links are symmetric;
face-cycle next links return to the original half-edge.

Appendix.Content: Vertex-manifoldness needs an additional fan test. Merely checking that every edge has at most two incident faces does not reject a “bow-tie” vertex whose incident triangles form separate fans touching only at that vertex.
Euler characteristic as a diagnostic
For a finite mesh complex,
Appendix.RawBlock: <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block"> <mi>χ</mi> <mo>=</mo> <mi>V</mi> <mo>−</mo> <mi>E</mi> <mo>+</mo> <mi>F</mi> <mo>.</mo> </math>
Appendix.Content: A topological disk has <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>χ</mi> <mo>=</mo> <mn>1</mn> </math>. A closed sphere-like tetrahedron has <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>χ</mi> <mo>=</mo> <mn>2</mn> </math>. Euler characteristic does not fully classify arbitrary meshes, but it is a powerful cross-check against adjacency construction.
Why topology must be separated from geometry

Two faces can be topologically adjacent even if their coordinates are nearly coincident or wildly deformed. Conversely, two spatially overlapping triangles need not share topology. Build connectivity from explicit vertex/edge identity unless the task is specifically to weld geometric duplicates under a tolerance.
Executable witness

tools/labs/mesh_topology_lab.cpp builds directed/undirected edge maps, pairs twins, counts boundaries and non-manifold edges, checks orientation, and validates Euler characteristic on a two-triangle disk and a closed tetrahedron. A third case deliberately creates a three-face non-manifold edge.
The witness does not yet prove vertex-fan manifoldness, polygonal faces, robust welding, edge collapse, remeshing or production importer parity.
Related: Half-edge mesh connectivity, Mesh topology and homology, QEM edge collapse and validity.

Appendix.title: Homogeneous clipping and perspective interpolation
Appendix.Content: Homogeneous clipping and perspective interpolation
Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: University courses · Latest development: University courses
Definition and mechanism

After a vertex is transformed, its clip-space coordinate is <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <msub> <mi>x</mi> <mi>c</mi> </msub> <mo>,</mo> <msub> <mi>y</mi> <mi>c</mi> </msub> <mo>,</mo> <msub> <mi>z</mi> <mi>c</mi> </msub> <mo>,</mo> <msub> <mi>w</mi> <mi>c</mi> </msub> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </math>. Clip primitives against the view volume before perspective division; under the conventional OpenGL clip convention the inequalities are <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mo>−</mo> <msub> <mi>w</mi> <mi>c</mi> </msub> <mo>≤</mo> <msub> <mi>x</mi> <mi>c</mi> </msub> <mo>,</mo> <msub> <mi>y</mi> <mi>c</mi> </msub> <mo>,</mo> <msub> <mi>z</mi> <mi>c</mi> </msub> <mo>≤</mo> <msub> <mi>w</mi> <mi>c</mi> </msub> </math>. A crossing edge is split by interpolating its homogeneous endpoints, which preserves the projective line and avoids dividing by a small or negative <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>w</mi> </math> too early. Only surviving points are divided by <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <msub> <mi>w</mi> <mi>c</mi> </msub> </math> to enter normalized device coordinates. Attributes then need perspective-correct interpolation: screen-space barycentric weights interpolate <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>a</mi> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"> <mo>/</mo> </mrow> <mi>w</mi> </math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mn>1</mn> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"> <mo>/</mo> </mrow> <mi>w</mi> </math>, and the fragment value is their ratio. For a triangle with weights <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <msub> <mi>λ</mi> <mi>i</mi> </msub> </math>, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>a</mi> <mo>=</mo> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <munder> <mo data-mjx-texclass="OP">∑</mo> <mi>i</mi> </munder> <msub> <mi>λ</mi> <mi>i</mi> </msub> <msub> <mi>a</mi> <mi>i</mi> </msub> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"> <mo>/</mo> </mrow> <msub> <mi>w</mi> <mi>i</mi> </msub> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"> <mo>/</mo> </mrow> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <munder> <mo data-mjx-texclass="OP">∑</mo> <mi>i</mi> </munder> <msub> <mi>λ</mi> <mi>i</mi> </msub> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"> <mo>/</mo> </mrow> <msub> <mi>w</mi> <mi>i</mi> </msub> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </math>. Direct linear interpolation in screen space is correct only for affine quantities or equal depth; otherwise textures warp. Clip-space depth conventions and the near/far interval vary by API and projection setup, so the inequalities must match the active pipeline.

Phase 11 camera development

Clipping and perspective-correct interpolation preserve projective geometry, while texture filtering asks how much surface area maps to a pixel. Neighboring camera rays approximate the image-to-surface footprint. At grazing angles one pixel can cover a long, thin region; a center-only texel lookup may alias detail even when attributes interpolate correctly. Use footprint estimates to select mip levels or anisotropic filters, while respecting visibility edges where derivatives jump. Ray differentials aid sampling but do not replace clipping or multisample coverage. Source basis: PBRT differential-ray texture filtering. Link: A camera model must close the loop; research: Four deeper links from the TUM lecture review.
Worked clip-plane trace beside the shader explanation

For clip endpoints <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mn>0</mn> <mo>,</mo> <mn>0</mn> <mo>,</mo> <mn>0</mn> <mo>,</mo> <mn>1</mn> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mn>6</mn> <mo>,</mo> <mn>0</mn> <mo>,</mo> <mn>0</mn> <mo>,</mo> <mn>2</mn> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </math>, the right-plane intersection uses homogeneous edge parameter <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mn>1</mn> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"> <mo>/</mo> </mrow> <mn>5</mn> </math>; interpolating the already divided endpoints would use <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mn>1</mn> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"> <mo>/</mo> </mrow> <mn>3</mn> </math>. The worked trace and pipeline figure also explain negative fourth components, the zero-divisor limit and declared depth conventions. This is used by the shader-stage teaching before program compilation and linking are discussed.
Executable raster-state continuation

The project now carries two complementary CPU witnesses. tools/labs/raster_reference_lab.cpp owns edge coverage, barycentrics, perspective-correct interpolation and depth ordering. tools/labs/raster_pipeline_state_lab.cpp continues the same pipeline through a homogeneous clip-plane intersection, an explicit four-sample coverage mask, stencil compare/pass update and premultiplied source-over blending.

That separation is deliberate: clipping happens in homogeneous coordinates before divide-by-<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>w</mi> </math>; sample ownership happens after screen mapping; stencil/depth are stateful per-fragment/sample decisions; blending combines a surviving source with an existing destination. Treating all of them as “rasterization” without preserving these boundaries makes debugging nearly impossible.

Appendix.title: Incremental contact penetration refresh
Appendix.Content: Incremental contact penetration refresh

Position correction moves every contact point attached to the corrected bodies. For a small rotation, its first-order point displacement is translation plus rotation vector crossed with the pre-correction world-space lever arm. Project the difference of the two point movements onto the frozen contact normal, using the declared normal and penetration signs.

Refresh each known contact once for the correction just applied, then reconsider the worst penetration. Reusing an old correction counts movement twice. This local estimate cannot discover new contacts or replace geometry refresh after substantial rotation or a feature change.
Prerequisites
Full teaching and executable evidence

Content.Link: Derivation, three-contact ranking trace and complexity limits

Appendix.Content: Used by
Iterative position correction and contact-priority updates. The reference is a frozen-feature updater, not a full collision detector or rigid-body solver.

Appendix.title: Lens optics and depth of field
Appendix.source: Concepts/Lens optics and depth of field.md
Appendix.Content: Lens optics and depth of field
Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: University courses · Latest development: University courses
Definition and mechanism

A pinhole camera maps every scene point to one image point through a single center, but a real lens has a finite aperture. Rays from one object point pass through different parts of the aperture and meet at a focused image point only for the chosen focus distance. Points nearer or farther from that plane form a blur disk called the circle of confusion. Stopping down the aperture narrows the cone of rays and increases depth of field, but reduces collected light and may require longer exposure or higher sensor gain. Focal length and focus distance also affect field of view and perspective magnification. A thin-lens model is an approximation; real lenses add aberrations and vignetting. The model helps explain why depth of field is both an optical effect and a sampling/integration process over aperture positions.
Prerequisites
Used by

Content.Link: Ray differentials and camera sampling measures

Appendix.Content: Full teaching explanation
Lens optics, focus, and image formation · Photographic composition, history, and communication · Photographic workflow and integrated decisions
Phase 11 camera development

A pinhole camera emits one ideal ray per image location. A finite-aperture lens samples a family of rays whose intersections form a blur disk away from the focal plane. A thin-lens camera therefore samples film and lens position, then aims through a focal point. Differentials from film offsets alone omit aperture variation unless the model includes it. Monte Carlo PDFs and camera weights must match the sampled film/aperture measure. The thin-lens model approximates real optics; aberrations and bokeh shape require richer models. Link: A camera model must close the loop; research: Four deeper links from the TUM lecture review.

Appendix.title: Local rigidity and mesh orientation fields
Appendix.source: Concepts/Local rigidity and mesh orientation fields.md
Appendix.Content: Local rigidity and mesh orientation fields
Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: University courses · Latest development: University courses
Definition and mechanism

As-Rigid-As-Possible (ARAP) deformation seeks vertex positions that change as little as possible from a preferred local rigid transform. For each vertex neighborhood, fit a rotation to the deformed edge vectors, then minimize residuals between transformed rest edges and current edges. Alternating between local rotations and a global position solve makes a nonlinear shape-editing problem tractable, but the result depends on constraints, initialization, mesh quality, and rotation fitting. Instant Meshes uses direction or orientation fields over a surface to guide a quad-dominant remeshing; field singularities encode where a globally consistent direction cannot exist. A mesh’s half-edge connectivity, boundary structure, and orientation determine valid neighborhoods and field transport. Poor triangles, seams, boundary conditions, or inconsistent orientation can create artifacts. ARAP is a local preservation objective, not exact rigidity of the whole shape; a direction field guides topology but does not uniquely determine a good mesh without sizing and feature constraints.
Prerequisites

Content.Link: Manifold polygon meshes and boundary structure

Appendix.title: Mesh topology and homology
Appendix.Content: Mesh topology and homology

Mesh geometry concerns positions, lengths, angles and curvature. Mesh topology concerns connectivity: which vertices belong to edges, which edges bound faces, which faces meet, where boundaries exist, and how many connected/loop/void structures the complex contains.
Two meshes can have very different coordinates and the same topology. Two triangles can overlap geometrically without being topologically adjacent if they do not share vertex/edge identity.
Simplicial-chain view
For a triangle mesh, vertices are 0-simplices, edges are 1-simplices and faces are 2-simplices. A chain is a formal linear combination of simplices.
Boundary operators satisfy
Appendix.RawBlock: <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block"> <msub> <mi>∂</mi> <mi>k</mi> </msub> <msub> <mi>∂</mi> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"> <mi>k</mi> <mo>+</mo> <mn>1</mn> </mrow> </msub> <mo>=</mo> <mn>0</mn> <mo>,</mo> </math>
Appendix.Content: the algebraic statement that “the boundary of a boundary is zero.”
Cycles are chains whose boundary vanishes. Boundaries are cycles created as the boundary of a higher-dimensional chain. Homology quotients cycles by boundaries:
Appendix.RawBlock: <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block"> <msub> <mi>H</mi> <mi>k</mi> </msub> <mo>=</mo> <msub> <mi>Z</mi> <mi>k</mi> </msub> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"> <mo>/</mo> </mrow> <msub> <mi>B</mi> <mi>k</mi> </msub> <mo>.</mo> </math>
Appendix.Content: The Betti number <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <msub> <mi>β</mi> <mi>k</mi> </msub> <mo>=</mo> <mi>dim</mi> <mo data-mjx-texclass="NONE">⁡</mo> <msub> <mi>H</mi> <mi>k</mi> </msub> </math> counts independent homology classes over the chosen coefficient field (for example, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <msub> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"> <mi mathvariant="double-struck">Z</mi> </mrow> <mn>2</mn> </msub> </math>); <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <msub> <mi>Z</mi> <mi>k</mi> </msub> </math> is the kernel of the <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>k</mi> </math>-boundary map and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <msub> <mi>B</mi> <mi>k</mi> </msub> </math> is the image of the <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mi>k</mi> <mo>+</mo> <mn>1</mn> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </math>-boundary map.

For a connected orientable closed surface, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <msub> <mi>β</mi> <mn>0</mn> </msub> <mo>=</mo> <mn>1</mn> </math>; <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <msub> <mi>β</mi> <mn>1</mn> </msub> </math> counts independent one-dimensional homology classes (for genus <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>g</mi> </math>, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <msub> <mi>β</mi> <mn>1</mn> </msub> <mo>=</mo> <mn>2</mn> <mi>g</mi> </math>); and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <msub> <mi>β</mi> <mn>2</mn> </msub> <mo>=</mo> <mn>1</mn> </math> represents the surface’s fundamental two-dimensional class. With a boundary, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <msub> <mi>β</mi> <mn>2</mn> </msub> </math> need not be one.
Euler characteristic
For a finite triangle complex with vertex, edge and face counts <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>V</mi> <mo>,</mo> <mi>E</mi> <mo>,</mo> <mi>F</mi> </math>,
Appendix.RawBlock: <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block"> <mi>χ</mi> <mo>=</mo> <mi>V</mi> <mo>−</mo> <mi>E</mi> <mo>+</mo> <mi>F</mi> <mo>.</mo> </math>
Appendix.Content: For a connected closed orientable surface of genus <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>g</mi> </math>,
Appendix.RawBlock: <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block"> <mi>χ</mi> <mo>=</mo> <mn>2</mn> <mo>−</mo> <mn>2</mn> <mi>g</mi> <mo>.</mo> </math>
Appendix.Content: But equal Euler characteristic alone does not prove arbitrary complexes are topologically equivalent. It is a checksum, not a complete classifier.
Mesh diagnostics
Topology checks used by a geometry pipeline should include:

ListItem.Content: boundary-edge count;
non-manifold edges with more than two incident faces;
inconsistent face orientation;
disconnected components;
vertex fan manifoldness;
isolated vertices/edges;
duplicate faces;
Euler characteristic and, where appropriate, homology.

Appendix.Content: tools/labs/mesh_topology_lab.cpp now gives an executable layer for unique edges, half-edge twins, boundary/non-manifold classification and Euler characteristic.
Read the connected explanation in Continuous Notes/University - Worlds, Images and Inference - Graphics, Vision and Photography#From a scanned triangle soup to a mesh we can trust.
Related: Half-edge topology invariants, Persistent homology, QEM edge collapse and validity.

Appendix.title: Microfacet normal distributions
Appendix.Content: Microfacet normal distributions

A microfacet model treats a macroscopically rough surface as a statistical collection of tiny planar facets. The normal distribution function <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>D</mi> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mi>m</mi> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </math> is not simply “the probability of a normal.” It measures the density of microfacet area oriented around direction <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>m</mi> </math> relative to the macroscopic surface.

For an isotropic GGX distribution with roughness parameter <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>a</mi> <mi>l</mi> <mi>p</mi> <mi>h</mi> <mi>a</mi> </math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>c</mi> <mo>=</mo> <mi>n</mi> <mo>⋅</mo> <mi>m</mi> </math>,
Appendix.RawBlock: <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block"> <msub> <mi>D</mi> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"> <mi>G</mi> <mi>G</mi> <mi>X</mi> </mrow> </msub> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mi>m</mi> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> <mo>=</mo> <mfrac> <msup> <mi>α</mi> <mn>2</mn> </msup> <mrow> <mi>π</mi> <msup> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="INNER"> <mo data-mjx-texclass="OPEN">[</mo> <msup> <mi>c</mi> <mn>2</mn> </msup> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <msup> <mi>α</mi> <mn>2</mn> </msup> <mo>−</mo> <mn>1</mn> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> <mo>+</mo> <mn>1</mn> <mo data-mjx-texclass="CLOSE">]</mo> </mrow> <mn>2</mn> </msup> </mrow> </mfrac> <mo>,</mo> <mstyle scriptlevel="0"> <mspace width="2em" /> </mstyle> <mi>c</mi> <mo>></mo> <mn>0.</mn> </math>
Appendix.Content: The important normalization is projected area:
Appendix.RawBlock: <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block"> <msub> <mo data-mjx-texclass="OP">∫</mo> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"> <msup> <mi mathvariant="normal">Ω</mi> <mo>+</mo> </msup> </mrow> </msub> <mi>D</mi> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mi>m</mi> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mi>n</mi> <mo>⋅</mo> <mi>m</mi> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> <mstyle scriptlevel="0"> <mspace width="0.167em" /> </mstyle> <mi>d</mi> <msub> <mi>ω</mi> <mi>m</mi> </msub> <mo>=</mo> <mn>1.</mn> </math>
Appendix.Content: That cosine factor is why <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>D</mi> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mi>m</mi> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </math> itself must not be substituted directly for a solid-angle sampling PDF without the transformation required by the sampling method.
From NDF to BRDF
For reflection, the half-vector is
Appendix.RawBlock: <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block"> <mi>h</mi> <mo>=</mo> <mfrac> <mrow> <msub> <mi>ω</mi> <mi>i</mi> </msub> <mo>+</mo> <msub> <mi>ω</mi> <mi>o</mi> </msub> </mrow> <mrow> <mo data-mjx-texclass="ORD" fence="false" stretchy="false">‖</mo> <msub> <mi>ω</mi> <mi>i</mi> </msub> <mo>+</mo> <msub> <mi>ω</mi> <mi>o</mi> </msub> <mo data-mjx-texclass="ORD" fence="false" stretchy="false">‖</mo> </mrow> </mfrac> <mo>.</mo> </math>
Appendix.Content: A common Cook–Torrance microfacet BRDF is
Appendix.RawBlock: <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block"> <msub> <mi>f</mi> <mi>r</mi> </msub> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <msub> <mi>ω</mi> <mi>i</mi> </msub> <mo>,</mo> <msub> <mi>ω</mi> <mi>o</mi> </msub> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> <mo>=</mo> <mfrac> <mrow> <mi>D</mi> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mi>h</mi> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> <mi>F</mi> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <msub> <mi>ω</mi> <mi>i</mi> </msub> <mo>,</mo> <mi>h</mi> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> <mi>G</mi> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <msub> <mi>ω</mi> <mi>i</mi> </msub> <mo>,</mo> <msub> <mi>ω</mi> <mi>o</mi> </msub> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </mrow> <mrow> <mn>4</mn> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mi>n</mi> <mo>⋅</mo> <msub> <mi>ω</mi> <mi>i</mi> </msub> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mi>n</mi> <mo>⋅</mo> <msub> <mi>ω</mi> <mi>o</mi> </msub> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </mrow> </mfrac> <mo>.</mo> </math>
Appendix.Content: Each factor has a different job. <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>D</mi> </math> describes facet orientation statistics. <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>F</mi> </math> describes Fresnel reflection. <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>G</mi> </math> accounts for masking and shadowing. The denominator converts the microfacet-area reasoning into a BRDF measured with respect to projected macroscopic area.

Confusing these roles produces common bugs: multiplying Fresnel twice, using roughness directly where <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>a</mi> <mi>l</mi> <mi>p</mi> <mi>h</mi> <mi>a</mi> <mo>=</mo> <mi>r</mi> <mi>o</mi> <mi>u</mi> <mi>g</mi> <mi>h</mi> <mi>n</mi> <mi>e</mi> <mi>s</mi> <msup> <mi>s</mi> <mn>2</mn> </msup> </math> was intended, or treating the NDF as the sampled-direction PDF.
Numerical behavior

At very low roughness, the GGX lobe becomes extremely concentrated. A finite-precision implementation needs a policy for minimum roughness, denominator protection, and tangent-frame validity. Simply adding an arbitrary epsilon everywhere changes the model and can break energy behavior.

At grazing angles, both the geometry term and the denominator become sensitive. The correct response is to derive the limiting behavior and use stable forms, not to clamp intermediate terms independently until the image looks plausible.
Executable reference

tools/labs/pbr_reference_lab.cpp numerically integrates the projected GGX normalization for several roughness values. It also checks Schlick Fresnel endpoint behavior and reciprocity/finiteness of an isotropic GGX + Smith BRDF.

Those checks establish mathematical contracts. They do not prove white-furnace energy conservation for the complete material model, anisotropic GGX, transmission, texture-space normal handling, or renderer parity.
Primary reading in the graphics volume: Continuous Notes/University - Worlds, Images and Inference - Graphics, Vision and Photography#Ask a surface where incoming energy can go.
Related: Multiple importance sampling, Color encoding and linear-light operations, Surface tangents normals and bitangents.
Extended executable reference

tools/labs/pbr_extended_reference_lab.cpp adds the cases that the first isotropic oracle explicitly left open. It numerically checks projected-area normalization for anisotropic GGX with independent tangent-axis roughness, evaluates exact dielectric Fresnel at normal and grazing limits, reconstructs Snell refraction including total internal reflection, and integrates a Lambertian material in a uniform white furnace.

The furnace check is intentionally modest: Lambertian reflection has an analytic target equal to albedo, making it an independent conservation oracle. It does not claim that a single-scattering rough microfacet reflection model automatically passes a furnace test at every roughness; multiple-scattering compensation and rough transmission need their own model-specific derivations and tests.

Appendix.title: Multiple importance sampling
Appendix.Content: Multiple importance sampling
Multiple importance sampling combines estimators from several sampling techniques without pretending that one proposal distribution is good everywhere.

Suppose two techniques generate the same contribution <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>f</mi> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mi>x</mi> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </math> using PDFs <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <msub> <mi>p</mi> <mi>a</mi> </msub> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mi>x</mi> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <msub> <mi>p</mi> <mi>b</mi> </msub> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mi>x</mi> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </math>. With one sample from each technique, an MIS estimator can use weights <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <msub> <mi>w</mi> <mi>a</mi> </msub> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mi>x</mi> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <msub> <mi>w</mi> <mi>b</mi> </msub> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mi>x</mi> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </math> satisfying appropriate partition and support conditions. The balance heuristic uses
Appendix.RawBlock: <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block"> <msub> <mi>w</mi> <mi>a</mi> </msub> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mi>x</mi> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> <mo>=</mo> <mfrac> <mrow> <msub> <mi>n</mi> <mi>a</mi> </msub> <msub> <mi>p</mi> <mi>a</mi> </msub> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mi>x</mi> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </mrow> <mrow> <msub> <mi>n</mi> <mi>a</mi> </msub> <msub> <mi>p</mi> <mi>a</mi> </msub> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mi>x</mi> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> <mo>+</mo> <msub> <mi>n</mi> <mi>b</mi> </msub> <msub> <mi>p</mi> <mi>b</mi> </msub> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mi>x</mi> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </mrow> </mfrac> <mo>,</mo> </math>
Appendix.Content: with the symmetric definition for <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <msub> <mi>w</mi> <mi>b</mi> </msub> </math>. For one sample from each, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <msub> <mi>n</mi> <mi>a</mi> </msub> <mo>=</mo> <msub> <mi>n</mi> <mi>b</mi> </msub> <mo>=</mo> <mn>1</mn> </math>.

The key idea is not “average two answers.” The estimator must evaluate the PDFs in the same measure for the same sampled event. Mixing a solid-angle PDF with an area PDF without the Jacobian conversion makes the weights meaningless.
Support matters

If technique A can sample a contribution that B cannot, then <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <msub> <mi>p</mi> <mi>b</mi> </msub> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mi>x</mi> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> <mo>=</mo> <mn>0</mn> </math> at that event and A should receive full weight. But if the implementation accidentally reports zero because it evaluated the wrong lobe, wrong hemisphere, or wrong light-selection probability, MIS can hide a bug behind a numerically finite result.
For direct lighting, the full light-sampling PDF may include both discrete light selection and continuous point/direction sampling:
Appendix.RawBlock: <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block"> <msub> <mi>p</mi> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"> <mi>l</mi> <mi>i</mi> <mi>g</mi> <mi>h</mi> <mi>t</mi> </mrow> </msub> <mo>=</mo> <mi>p</mi> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mtext>choose light</mtext> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> <mstyle scriptlevel="0"> <mspace width="0.167em" /> </mstyle> <mi>p</mi> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mtext>sample point or direction</mtext> <mo>∣</mo> <mtext>light</mtext> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> <mo>.</mo> </math>
Appendix.Content: The BSDF PDF must be converted to the same directional measure before comparison.
Power heuristic
A common alternative is
Appendix.RawBlock: <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block"> <msub> <mi>w</mi> <mi>a</mi> </msub> <mo>=</mo> <mfrac> <mrow> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <msub> <mi>n</mi> <mi>a</mi> </msub> <msub> <mi>p</mi> <mi>a</mi> </msub> <msup> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> <mi>β</mi> </msup> </mrow> <mrow> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <msub> <mi>n</mi> <mi>a</mi> </msub> <msub> <mi>p</mi> <mi>a</mi> </msub> <msup> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> <mi>β</mi> </msup> <mo>+</mo> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <msub> <mi>n</mi> <mi>b</mi> </msub> <msub> <mi>p</mi> <mi>b</mi> </msub> <msup> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> <mi>β</mi> </msup> </mrow> </mfrac> <mo>,</mo> </math>
Appendix.Content: often with <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>β</mi> <mo>=</mo> <mn>2</mn> </math>. This suppresses a technique more aggressively when its PDF is much smaller than the competing proposal.
The heuristic changes variance, not the target integral, when the estimator is constructed correctly.
Executable reference

tools/labs/monte_carlo_transport_lab.cpp checks the simple balance-weight partition property and separately verifies cosine-hemisphere transport and Russian-roulette expectation compensation. It is a mathematical estimator witness, not yet a complete path tracer with next-event estimation and scene lights.
Read the connected derivation at Continuous Notes/University - Worlds, Images and Inference - Graphics, Vision and Photography#Follow one path without losing its probability.
Related: Russian roulette path termination, Inverse, rejection, and importance sampling, Sampling support and missing strata.
Scene-level MIS witness

tools/labs/path_transport_scene_lab.cpp lifts the estimator checks into an actual camera/geometry/shading path. A camera ray intersects a sphere, establishes the shading normal, and evaluates Lambertian outgoing radiance under a constant environment using two proposals for the same hemisphere integral: uniform-hemisphere light sampling and cosine-weighted BSDF sampling. Each sample evaluates both PDFs in the same solid-angle measure and uses the balance heuristic.
Because constant environment radiance over a Lambertian surface has the analytic solution
Appendix.RawBlock: <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block"> <msub> <mi>L</mi> <mi>o</mi> </msub> <mo>=</mo> <mi>ρ</mi> <msub> <mi>L</mi> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"> <mi>e</mi> <mi>n</mi> <mi>v</mi> </mrow> </msub> <mo>,</mo> </math>
Appendix.Content: the pixel estimate has an independent target rather than merely comparing two noisy implementations. The witness therefore checks geometry, throughput, proposal PDFs, MIS weighting and convergence together. Emissive-geometry NEE, multiple bounces, media and full rendered-image parity remain later evidence layers.

Appendix.title: Persistent homology
Appendix.Content: Persistent homology

Ordinary homology asks which connected components, loops and higher-dimensional voids exist in one topological complex. Persistent homology asks how those features appear and disappear as a scale or threshold changes.
Begin with a filtration:
Appendix.RawBlock: <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block"> <msub> <mi>K</mi> <mn>0</mn> </msub> <mo>⊆</mo> <msub> <mi>K</mi> <mn>1</mn> </msub> <mo>⊆</mo> <mo>⋯</mo> <mo>⊆</mo> <msub> <mi>K</mi> <mi>m</mi> </msub> <mo>.</mo> </math>
Appendix.Content: Each step adds vertices, edges, faces or higher cells according to a declared rule. A topological feature is born when it first appears and dies when it becomes a boundary or merges according to the homology pairing convention.
Its persistence is often summarized by an interval
Appendix.RawBlock: <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block"> <mo stretchy="false">[</mo> <mi>b</mi> <mo>,</mo> <mi>d</mi> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </math>
Appendix.Content: or a point <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mi>b</mi> <mo>,</mo> <mi>d</mi> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </math> in a persistence diagram.
What persistence means

A long-lived feature is stable across a wider range of the chosen filtration parameter. That can make it more robust to one class of perturbation, but it is not proof that the feature is physically meaningful. The conclusion depends on:

ListItem.Content: the distance or scalar field used;
sampling density;
noise/outlier model;
complex construction such as Vietoris–Rips, Čech or alpha complex;
coefficient field;
filtration scale.

Appendix.Content: A persistent loop in a noisy scan can reflect real geometry, a sampling hole, or the behavior of the chosen complex.
Union-find intuition for H0

For connected components, persistence can be understood with disjoint sets. Vertices are born as components. When an edge connects two previously separate components, one component dies at that edge’s filtration value according to a consistent elder-rule convention.
Higher-dimensional persistence requires boundary-matrix reduction or more specialized algorithms.
Mesh/reconstruction relevance

Persistent homology can help diagnose captured geometry across thresholds: which holes survive changing reconstruction confidence, neighborhood radius or density? That is a better use than quoting a Betti number from one arbitrary threshold.
A study should compare the persistence structure with controlled synthetic holes/noise so the interpretation is calibrated.
Evidence boundary

The repository’s mathematics expansion develops complexes, chains, boundaries, Betti reasoning and persistence concepts. It does not yet claim a production-scale persistent-homology solver or a theorem that a persistent feature corresponds to a physically correct surface.
Read the connected explanation in Continuous Notes/University - Worlds, Images and Inference - Graphics, Vision and Photography#From a scanned triangle soup to a mesh we can trust.
Related: Mesh topology and homology, Half-edge topology invariants.

Appendix.title: Perspective-correct interpolation
Appendix.Content: Perspective-correct interpolation

Rasterization computes barycentric coordinates in screen space, but many vertex attributes are defined as linear functions on the original 3D primitive before perspective division. Directly interpolating those attributes with screen-space barycentrics therefore produces the wrong result.

Let clip-space vertex <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>i</mi> </math> have homogeneous coordinate <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <msub> <mi>w</mi> <mi>i</mi> </msub> </math> and attribute <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <msub> <mi>a</mi> <mi>i</mi> </msub> </math>. If screen-space barycentric weights at a sample are <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <msub> <mi>λ</mi> <mi>i</mi> </msub> </math>, perspective-correct interpolation is
Appendix.RawBlock: <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block"> <mi>a</mi> <mo>=</mo> <mfrac> <mrow> <munder> <mo data-mjx-texclass="OP">∑</mo> <mi>i</mi> </munder> <msub> <mi>λ</mi> <mi>i</mi> </msub> <msub> <mi>a</mi> <mi>i</mi> </msub> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"> <mo>/</mo> </mrow> <msub> <mi>w</mi> <mi>i</mi> </msub> </mrow> <mrow> <munder> <mo data-mjx-texclass="OP">∑</mo> <mi>i</mi> </munder> <msub> <mi>λ</mi> <mi>i</mi> </msub> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"> <mo>/</mo> </mrow> <msub> <mi>w</mi> <mi>i</mi> </msub> </mrow> </mfrac> <mo>.</mo> </math>
Appendix.Content: The denominator reconstructs the projective scaling that was lost during perspective division.
Why affine screen interpolation fails

Imagine two vertices at different depths but carrying texture coordinates that vary linearly across the original triangle. Perspective makes equal screen distances correspond to unequal distances on the surface. Affine screen interpolation assumes the opposite, so textures visibly “swim” or warp across polygons.

The derivation can be viewed by interpolating homogeneous quantities before division: both <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>a</mi> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"> <mo>/</mo> </mrow> <mi>w</mi> </math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mn>1</mn> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"> <mo>/</mo> </mrow> <mi>w</mi> </math> are affine in screen barycentrics, then dividing recovers <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>a</mi> </math>.
Depth is a separate contract

Do not blindly apply the same formula to every quantity named “depth.” Hardware depth after projection/divide is designed to interpolate affinely in screen space under the pipeline’s projective construction. Camera-space <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>z</mi> </math>, Euclidean range and reciprocal depth are different quantities.
The shader/runtime must know which one it is carrying.
Derivatives

Texture gradients used for mip/anisotropic filtering are derivatives of the perspective-correct attribute with respect to screen position. Finite differences across neighboring fragments approximate that quotient behavior; manually reconstructing derivatives requires differentiating the quotient rather than differentiating the raw affine numerator alone.
Executable reference

tools/labs/raster_reference_lab.cpp chooses a triangle with unequal reciprocal-w values and verifies that affine interpolation differs from the perspective-correct result. The same lab tests top-left edge ownership and depth ordering.
Teach and reconstruct: Continuous Notes/University - Worlds, Images and Inference - Graphics, Vision and Photography#Decide which samples a triangle owns.
Related: Homogeneous clipping and perspective interpolation, Reversed-Z depth contracts.

Appendix.title: Probability density and change of measure
Appendix.source: Concepts/Probability density and change of measure.md
Appendix.Content: Probability density and change of measure
Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: University courses · Latest development: Phase 10
Definition and mechanism

A probability density describes probability per unit of a chosen measure, not probability at a point. A density <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <msub> <mi>p</mi> <mi>A</mi> </msub> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mi>a</mi> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </math> over area differs from a density <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <msub> <mi>p</mi> <mi>ω</mi> </msub> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mi>ω</mi> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </math> over solid angle. When a mapping changes variables, its Jacobian converts density so total probability remains one: <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <msub> <mi>p</mi> <mi>B</mi> </msub> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mi>b</mi> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> <mo>=</mo> <msub> <mi>p</mi> <mi>A</mi> </msub> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mi>a</mi> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"> <mo stretchy="false">|</mo> </mrow> <mi>d</mi> <mi>a</mi> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"> <mo>/</mo> </mrow> <mi>d</mi> <mi>b</mi> <mo stretchy="false">|</mo> </math> in one dimension, with the determinant of the inverse Jacobian in multiple dimensions. In rendering, choosing a point on a light and using its direction from a shading point requires an area-to-solid-angle conversion involving distance squared and the light’s projected cosine. Estimator formulas are only correct when the sampling density and integral use the same measure. This concept prevents missing factors in importance sampling, environment-map sampling, and camera-lens integration.
Phase 9–10 development

A density is meaningful relative to a measure and its support; its value at a point is not itself an event probability. For a continuous scalar variable, an interval probability is the integral of the density over that interval. Under a differentiable one-to-one change of variables, the transformed density includes the absolute determinant of the inverse Jacobian. Values outside the transformed support have zero probability. A mixed law can contain both point masses and a continuous part, so one PDF alone cannot describe every distribution. When a renderer changes a surface-area density into a solid-angle density, the geometric Jacobian must preserve the same probability.
Prerequisites
Used by

Appendix.title: QEM edge collapse and validity
Appendix.Content: QEM edge collapse and validity

Mesh simplification is not “remove the shortest edge.” A collapse changes both geometry and topology, so a useful cost must estimate geometric error while a validity gate protects the mesh from illegal connectivity or orientation changes.
Plane quadrics
For a face plane
Appendix.RawBlock: <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block"> <mi>a</mi> <mi>x</mi> <mo>+</mo> <mi>b</mi> <mi>y</mi> <mo>+</mo> <mi>c</mi> <mi>z</mi> <mo>+</mo> <mi>d</mi> <mo>=</mo> <mn>0</mn> </math>
Appendix.Content: with normalized normal <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mi>a</mi> <mo>,</mo> <mi>b</mi> <mo>,</mo> <mi>c</mi> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </math>, write the homogeneous plane vector

Appendix.Content: The squared distance-like penalty of homogeneous vertex <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"> <mover> <mi>v</mi> <mo stretchy="false">¯</mo> </mover> </mrow> <mo>=</mo> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mi>x</mi> <mo>,</mo> <mi>y</mi> <mo>,</mo> <mi>z</mi> <mo>,</mo> <mn>1</mn> <msup> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"> <mi mathvariant="sans-serif">T</mi> </mrow> </mrow> </msup> </math> to that plane is
Appendix.RawBlock: <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block"> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <msup> <mi>p</mi> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"> <mi mathvariant="sans-serif">T</mi> </mrow> </mrow> </msup> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"> <mover> <mi>v</mi> <mo stretchy="false">¯</mo> </mover> </mrow> <msup> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> <mn>2</mn> </msup> <mo>=</mo> <msup> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"> <mover> <mi>v</mi> <mo stretchy="false">¯</mo> </mover> </mrow> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"> <mi mathvariant="sans-serif">T</mi> </mrow> </mrow> </msup> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mi>p</mi> <msup> <mi>p</mi> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"> <mi mathvariant="sans-serif">T</mi> </mrow> </mrow> </msup> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"> <mover> <mi>v</mi> <mo stretchy="false">¯</mo> </mover> </mrow> <mo>.</mo> </math>
Appendix.Content: So the face contributes quadric
Appendix.RawBlock: <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block"> <msub> <mi>K</mi> <mi>p</mi> </msub> <mo>=</mo> <mi>p</mi> <msup> <mi>p</mi> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"> <mi mathvariant="sans-serif">T</mi> </mrow> </mrow> </msup> <mo>.</mo> </math>
Appendix.Content: Sum incident face quadrics around a vertex. For candidate edge <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mi>u</mi> <mo>,</mo> <mi>v</mi> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </math>, combine
Appendix.RawBlock: <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block"> <mi>Q</mi> <mo>=</mo> <msub> <mi>Q</mi> <mi>u</mi> </msub> <mo>+</mo> <msub> <mi>Q</mi> <mi>v</mi> </msub> <mo>.</mo> </math>
Appendix.Content: Evaluate a proposed replacement position <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"> <mover> <mi>x</mi> <mo stretchy="false">¯</mo> </mover> </mrow> </math> using
Appendix.RawBlock: <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block"> <mi>E</mi> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mi>x</mi> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> <mo>=</mo> <msup> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"> <mover> <mi>x</mi> <mo stretchy="false">¯</mo> </mover> </mrow> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"> <mi mathvariant="sans-serif">T</mi> </mrow> </mrow> </msup> <mi>Q</mi> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"> <mover> <mi>x</mi> <mo stretchy="false">¯</mo> </mover> </mrow> <mo>.</mo> </math>
Appendix.Content: The optimal unconstrained position comes from the upper-left linear system when it is nonsingular. If that solve is unstable or singular, candidates such as endpoints and midpoint provide robust fallbacks.
Topology gate before cost
A low QEM cost does not make a collapse legal. Before committing, check conditions such as:

ListItem.Content: the link condition or equivalent local-manifold test;
boundary preservation policy;
no face becomes degenerate by repeated vertex identity;
no surviving triangle flips orientation beyond the chosen geometric tolerance;
attributes/seams that the simplifier promises to preserve;
no non-manifold edge or vertex is created.

Appendix.Content: The exact validity policy depends on whether the pipeline allows topology changes, but it must be explicit.
Priority queue invalidation

A simplifier often keeps edge candidates in a heap. After one collapse, nearby quadrics/connectivity change, so old candidate costs become stale. Use version stamps/generations or recompute on pop. Otherwise a heap can return a numerically small cost for an edge that no longer exists in the same neighborhood.
Verification

Compare simplification against invariants after every collapse: manifold/boundary status, valid indices, nonzero face area, finite coordinates and expected Euler behavior. Geometry error should be measured on the resulting surface rather than inferred only from the sum of local QEM costs.

The current branch now provides tools/labs/mesh_topology_lab.cpp for the topology layer and the existing cotangent-energy witness for discrete operators. A full executable QEM collapse loop remains the next implementation milestone rather than being silently claimed complete.
Related: Half-edge topology invariants, Mesh topology and homology.
Executable collapse layer

tools/labs/qem_edge_collapse_lab.cpp now implements the first complete QEM collapse witness instead of leaving this section at topology-only prose. It constructs normalized face planes, accumulates <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>p</mi> <msup> <mi>p</mi> <mi>T</mi> </msup> </math> quadrics into vertices, combines the two endpoint quadrics for an edge, evaluates candidate cost in homogeneous coordinates, and runs a geometric validity gate before accepting the collapse.

The validity witness deliberately distinguishes a triangle that disappears because it contains both collapsed endpoints from a surviving triangle that becomes degenerate or flips. The former is expected topology change; the latter is rejected. This still leaves the optimal <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mn>3</mn> <mo>×</mo> <mn>3</mn> </math> solve, link-condition proof, boundary-feature weights, attribute quadrics and progressive-mesh bookkeeping as higher layers, but QEM is no longer merely named.
Optimal solve and topology link-condition continuation
tools/labs/qem_optimal_link_lab.cpp now adds two pieces that the first collapse witness deliberately left open.

For a summed quadric written in homogeneous form, the candidate minimizing the quadratic error satisfies the <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mn>3</mn> <mo>×</mo> <mn>3</mn> </math> linear system formed by the upper-left block and translation column. The lab solves that system with pivoting, verifies the unique intersection of three orthogonal planes, and detects a rank-deficient single-plane quadric so the caller can fall back to an endpoint/midpoint policy instead of inventing an unstable inverse.

The same witness constructs vertex one-rings and the set of vertices opposite an edge in its incident triangles. A manifold triangle-mesh edge is accepted only when it has one boundary face or two interior faces and the common one-ring neighbors match that opposite set. A three-face edge is explicitly rejected as non-manifold. Attribute quadrics, boundary-feature weighting, priority-queue updates and production progressive simplification still remain above this reference layer.

Appendix.title: Reservoir resampling and ReSTIR
Appendix.Content: Reservoir resampling and ReSTIR
Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: University courses · Latest development: University courses
Definition and mechanism

Reservoir sampling keeps a compact candidate for a weighted distribution without storing every sample. When candidate <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <msub> <mi>y</mi> <mi>i</mi> </msub> </math> has target weight <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <msub> <mi>w</mi> <mi>i</mi> </msub> </math>, maintain a running weight sum and replace the stored candidate with probability proportional to <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <msub> <mi>w</mi> <mi>i</mi> </msub> </math>; the reservoir records enough normalization information to estimate the desired integral without bias under stated assumptions. ReSTIR reuses candidates across pixels and frames, which is valuable when direct lighting has many possible lights or paths but only a few can be evaluated per pixel. Reuse requires correcting for the source and target distributions, accounting for visibility changes, and managing temporal history. If weights or normalization are wrong, the image may be biased; stale reuse causes trails or light leaks when geometry or illumination moves. The method reduces expensive samples rather than making sampling free. It depends on a valid estimator, careful normalization, and an understanding of whether correlated reused samples preserve the intended expectation.

Appendix.title: Reversed-Z depth contracts
Appendix.Content: Reversed-Z depth contracts

A depth buffer stores an ordering coordinate, not Euclidean distance. Reversed-Z changes the mapping so near geometry receives larger depth values and far geometry approaches zero. The precision advantage comes from combining the reciprocal structure of perspective depth with floating-point numbers whose representable values are denser near zero.
The entire renderer has to agree on the convention. Reversing only the projection matrix while keeping old clear/comparison assumptions creates a system that is internally contradictory.
Contract checklist
For a conventional zero-to-one API depth range, a common reversed-Z setup uses:

ListItem.Content: near plane mapped near 1;
far distance mapped toward 0;
depth buffer cleared to 0;
comparison set to GREATER or GREATER_EQUAL;
hierarchical depth/occlusion reductions defined consistently with “larger is nearer”;
screen-space reconstruction derived from the exact projection convention.

Appendix.Content: Infinite-far reversed projection can remove an explicit far-plane distance from the perspective matrix, but frustum/culling policy still needs a practical world-space bound when the application cannot process infinite geometry.
Why floating point helps

Perspective depth is approximately affine in <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mn>1</mn> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"> <mo>/</mo> </mrow> <mi>z</mi> </math>. Conventional mapping spends many floating-point representable values near depth one, where far geometry is crowded. Reversed-Z places far geometry near zero, where floating-point exponent scaling gives much more useful relative spacing.
With integer/fixed-point depth, reversal alone does not create the same dramatic distribution advantage; the floating-point representation is part of the argument.
Reconstruction must use the actual matrix
Do not paste a “linearize depth” formula from another API. Different clip-space ranges, handedness, finite/infinite far planes and reversed mappings change the coefficients.
A robust reconstruction derives camera-space position from the same projection matrix or stores explicit projection parameters and tests known near/far points.
Occlusion and temporal systems

Hierarchical Z, SSAO, SSR, clustered depth slicing, picking and temporal rejection all consume depth meaning. Every reduction or comparison must be audited when the convention changes. A min-reduction hierarchy written for standard depth may need a max-reduction interpretation under reversed-Z.
Tests

Project known camera-space depths, confirm monotonic ordering, quantize them to the real depth format, reconstruct them, and measure relative world-space error over logarithmically spaced distances. Also test clear-value behavior with an empty frame and a near geometry sample.
Teach and reconstruct: Continuous Notes/University - Worlds, Images and Inference - Graphics, Vision and Photography#Give depth an explicit meaning.
Related: Hardware depth-buffer linearization, Rendering history validity.

Appendix.title: Russian roulette path termination
Appendix.Content: Russian roulette path termination

Russian roulette reduces expected path length without deterministically deleting every long path. At a continuation point, choose a survival probability <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>p</mi> <mo>∈</mo> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mn>0</mn> <mo>,</mo> <mn>1</mn> <mo stretchy="false">]</mo> </math>. If the path terminates, its future contribution is zero. If it survives, divide the surviving throughput by <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>p</mi> </math>.
For a continuation contribution <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>X</mi> </math>,
Appendix.RawBlock: <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block"> <mi>Y</mi> <mo>=</mo> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="INNER"> <mo data-mjx-texclass="OPEN">{</mo> <mtable columnalign="left left" columnspacing="1em" rowspacing=".2em"> <mtr> <mtd> <mi>X</mi> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"> <mo>/</mo> </mrow> <mi>p</mi> <mo>,</mo> </mtd> <mtd> <mtext>with probability </mtext> <mi>p</mi> <mo>,</mo> </mtd> </mtr> <mtr> <mtd> <mn>0</mn> <mo>,</mo> </mtd> <mtd> <mtext>with probability </mtext> <mn>1</mn> <mo>−</mo> <mi>p</mi> <mo>.</mo> </mtd> </mtr> </mtable> <mo data-mjx-texclass="CLOSE" fence="true" stretchy="true" symmetric="true" /> </mrow> </math>
Appendix.Content: Then
Appendix.RawBlock: <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block"> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"> <mi mathvariant="double-struck">E</mi> </mrow> <mo stretchy="false">[</mo> <mi>Y</mi> <mo stretchy="false">]</mo> <mo>=</mo> <mi>p</mi> <mfrac> <mi>X</mi> <mi>p</mi> </mfrac> <mo>+</mo> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mn>1</mn> <mo>−</mo> <mi>p</mi> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> <mn>0</mn> <mo>=</mo> <mi>X</mi> <mo>.</mo> </math>
Appendix.Content: The compensation preserves the continuation expectation. It does not guarantee lower variance, and it does not undo bias from a separate hard bounce cap.
Choosing the survival probability

A common design bases <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>p</mi> </math> on remaining throughput magnitude, usually after a minimum depth. But the exact scalar used—maximum channel, luminance-like measure, spectral bound—changes variance and path behavior. Clamp policies must be documented.

A very small <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>p</mi> </math> creates rare, very large weights <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mn>1</mn> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"> <mo>/</mo> </mrow> <mi>p</mi> </math>, which can increase variance dramatically. A <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>p</mi> </math> too close to one saves little work. The point is an efficiency trade-off, not a ritual after N bounces.
Conditional probability matters

The compensation uses the probability of surviving at that decision, conditioned on the path state that reached it. If the probability changes per bounce, multiply the path throughput by the reciprocal of each actual survival probability encountered. Do not divide later by a generic average probability.
Executable reference

tools/labs/monte_carlo_transport_lab.cpp runs one million deterministic-seed roulette trials and verifies that the sample mean remains close to the un-terminated contribution after survival compensation.
That does not prove a complete renderer. It isolates the stochastic invariant so a path tracer can test roulette independently of geometry, BSDF and light-sampling bugs.
Read the connected derivation at Continuous Notes/University - Worlds, Images and Inference - Graphics, Vision and Photography#Follow one path without losing its probability.
Related: Multiple importance sampling, Reproducible numerical benchmarking.

Appendix.title: Sampling support and missing strata
Appendix.Content: Sampling support and missing strata

The support of a sampling distribution is the set of outcomes it can generate with nonzero probability. Importance sampling can change how often regions are visited, but it cannot estimate a nonzero contribution from a region that the estimator never samples unless another technique covers that region.
For an integral
