This is strong preservation/formatting evidence, not a semantic certification of every previously existing paragraph, every math derivation, or every code block. The new differential lab tools/labs/disk_event_broadphase_differential_lab.cpp compares full world outcomes in exhaustive and swept-pair modes: event/batch counts, elapsed step time, stable identity, final positions and velocities. It includes four explicit scenes and 2,000 reproducibly seeded isolated impacts. The strict and UBSan contact workflow now references the lab. The test source and test registration were verified in GitHub; their execution status must be tied to a named hosted CI job or an exact-source local compile, never inferred from presence. General C++ CI diagnosis. The original .github/workflows/allmight-cpp20-labs.yml was returning immediately failed, zero-job Actions runs. Comparing it with the earlier successfully scheduled workflow identified only two added path-trigger lines referring to the legacy Computing Foundations note. The two-line edit was reverted byte-identically to the previously job-schedulable version, without removing any lab tests. GitHub then scheduled the matrix normally under workflow run 43127394396. Final job conclusions should be read independently from that run before claiming all compiler configurations passed. Scope and completeness boundary. The canonical Mathematics, Graphics and Game Engine notes are the implementation-first reader route; their supplements and standalone code are independent evidence artifacts, not substitutes for essential first-use teaching. The former Computing Foundations volume remains preserved as raw provenance; its complete source body has since been mechanically embedded by subject into Game Engine and Graphics. Semantic integration and first-use ordering are still being audited. The 3,000-part original curriculum, unread textbook chapters, unfinished caption/source review, and unverified real Kairo/GPU runtime paths remain open. A concept is not complete merely because its name or part number appears; it needs its derivation, conventions, state, executable algorithm, trace, failure cases and reproduced tests inside the relevant continuous narrative. Appendix.title: Cross-volume companion reference
Appendix.Content: This companion appears in Volume 2, The Foundations Bible — Volume II: Numerical Methods, Probability, Geometry and Camera Systems: Bandit exploration and regret — Bandit exploration and regret A multi-armed bandit models sequential choices when only the reward of the chosen action is observed. It separates exploitation—choosing what currently looks best—from exploration—choosing an uncertain action to learn about it. Let arm <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>a</mi> </math> have unknown mean reward <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <msub> <mi>μ</mi> <mi>a</mi> </msub> </math>. Over <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>T</mi> </math> rounds, one common stationary pseudo-regret benchmark is <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block"> <msub> <mi>R</mi> <mi>T</mi> </msub> <mo>=</mo> <mi>T</mi> <msup> <mi>μ</mi> <mo>∗</mo> </msup> <mo>−</mo> <munderover> <mo data-mjx-texclass="OP">∑</mo> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"> <mi>t</mi> <mo>=</mo> <mn>1</mn> </mrow> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"> <mi>T</mi> </mrow> </munderover> <msub> <mi>μ</mi> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"> <msub> <mi>A</mi> <mi>t</mi> </msub> </mrow> </msub> <mo>,</mo> </math> where <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <msup> <mi>μ</mi> <mo>∗</mo> </msup> </math> is the largest fixed-arm mean and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <msub> <mi>A</mi> <mi>t</mi> </msub> </math> is the chosen arm at round <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>t</mi> </math>. Regret is meaningful only relative to the benchmark and environment assumptions. In a nonstationary problem, “best fixed arm” may be the wrong target. UCB intuition Upper-confidence-bound methods choose an action using an optimistic estimate such as <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block"> <msub> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"> <mover> <mi>μ</mi> <mo stretchy="false">^</mo> </mover> </mrow> <mi>a</mi> </msub> <mo>+</mo> <mi>c</mi> <msqrt> <mfrac> <mrow> <mi>log</mi> <mo data-mjx-texclass="NONE">⁡</mo> <mi>t</mi> </mrow> <msub> <mi>N</mi> <mi>a</mi> </msub> </mfrac> </msqrt> <mo>,</mo> </math> where <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <msub> <mi>N</mi> <mi>a</mi> </msub> </math> is the number of samples from arm <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>a</mi> </math>. The uncertainty bonus shrinks with evidence and is larger for rarely tried arms. The derivation of a confidence radius depends on reward bounds/noise assumptions. Reusing a textbook radius for arbitrary unbounded timing noise or correlated frame measurements removes the theorem that motivated it. Nonstationary workloads Render cost, network latency, cache behavior and user demand can change. An all-history mean adapts slowly after a regime shift. Sliding-window estimates, exponential discounting or explicit change detection trade statistical efficiency in stationary periods for responsiveness. Adaptive sampling can change an estimator Choosing what to measure next based on observed rewards is useful for experimental efficiency, but it can make a naive final average biased toward frequently selected outcomes. Adaptive experiment allocation and unbiased Monte Carlo integration are different problems. When selection probabilities are known, importance weighting can correct some adaptive sampling schemes: <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block"> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"> <mover> <mi>μ</mi> <mo stretchy="false">^</mo> </mover> </mrow> <mo>=</mo> <mfrac> <mn>1</mn> <mi>T</mi> </mfrac> <munder> <mo data-mjx-texclass="OP">∑</mo> <mi>t</mi> </munder> <mfrac> <mrow> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"> <mn mathvariant="bold">1</mn> </mrow> <mo stretchy="false">[</mo> <msub> <mi>A</mi> <mi>t</mi> </msub> <mo>=</mo> <mi>a</mi> <mo stretchy="false">]</mo> <msub> <mi>X</mi> <mi>t</mi> </msub> </mrow> <mrow> <msub> <mi>p</mi> <mi>t</mi> </msub> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mi>a</mi> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </mrow> </mfrac> <mo>.</mo> </math> Very small selection probabilities can make the variance enormous, so mathematical unbiasedness does not guarantee a practical estimator. Graphics/research use Bandits are plausible for choosing which configuration to benchmark, which reconstruction region deserves another expensive measurement, or which experiment to run next. They should not be inserted into a pixel estimator on the assumption that maximizing a reward signal automatically preserves the target rendering integral. The direct mathematics expansion is at Continuous Notes/Computing Foundations - From Bits to C++ and Systems APIs#Choose the next measurement using the geometry of what is still unknown. The graphics narrative connects adaptive computation at Continuous Notes/University - Worlds, Images and Inference - Graphics, Vision and Photography#From Random Samples to Deliberate Computation. Related: Confidence intervals and sequential evidence, Inverse, rejection, and importance sampling, Sampling support and missing strata.. Open Bandit exploration and regret in Volume 2

Appendix.Content:
This companion appears in Volume 2, The Visual Computing Bible — Volume II: Computational Geometry, Vision, Reconstruction and XR: Camera calibration and bundle adjustment — Camera calibration and bundle adjustment Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: University courses · Latest development: University courses Definition and mechanism Camera calibration estimates parameters that map 3D points to image coordinates. Intrinsics describe focal scale, principal point, and lens distortion; extrinsics describe camera pose relative to the scene. Known calibration targets provide 3D-to-2D correspondences, and a nonlinear least-squares objective minimizes reprojection error. Bundle adjustment jointly refines many camera poses and 3D feature points by minimizing all observed image residuals. The problem is sparse because each image sees only a subset of points. It also has gauge freedoms: translating or scaling the entire reconstruction may leave projections unchanged, so fix a reference pose or scale. Robust loss functions reduce the effect of mismatched features. Good initialization, parameter scaling, and Jacobian structure determine whether optimization converges. Prerequisites
Homogeneous coordinates and perspective division Singular value decomposition
Used by
Worlds, Images and Inference Stereo correspondence and epipolar geometry Radiance fields and Gaussian splatting Off-axis stereo projection and disparity Omnidirectional camera projections Position reconstruction from depth Camera gauge freedoms and observability
Full teaching explanation Cameras, projection, and calibration · Pose estimation, transforms, and robust fitting · Stereo, relative orientation, and reconstruction Phase 11 camera development Linearize reprojection residuals as r(θ+δ)≈r(θ)+Jδ; the weighted information matrix <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <msup> <mi>J</mi> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"> <mi mathvariant="sans-serif">T</mi> </mrow> </mrow> </msup> <mi>W</mi> <mi>J</mi> </math> reveals parameter combinations that change observations. Null directions are local ambiguities, while small eigenvalues indicate weak constraints. In calibrated monocular structure from motion, global frame choice and common scene scale are gauge freedoms. Fix a pose and scale convention, or add a metric measurement, before interpreting covariance. Repeated nearly identical views may leave focal length, depth, and pose coupled even with many pixels. Link: A camera model must close the loop; research: Four deeper links from the TUM lecture review.. Open Camera calibration and bundle adjustment in Volume 2

This companion appears in Volume 2, The Visual Computing Bible — Volume II: Computational Geometry, Vision, Reconstruction and XR: Antialiasing and sample allocation — Antialiasing and sample allocation Curriculum depth: Introduced · First seen: XR01 · Latest development: Phase 10 Definition and mechanism SSAA increases spatial observations; MSAA principally adds coverage-related sampling under its shading conventions. TAA reuses aligned temporal observations. Nonlinear shading makes pre-/post-filtering noncommutative, so coarse rates need appropriate input/output policies. Phase 9–10 development Antialiasing combines a sampling pattern with a reconstruction or integration footprint so unresolved variation contributes with controlled error. More samples can reduce Monte Carlo variance, while better placement can reduce structured error; these are different effects. Adaptive allocation based on observed samples changes the sampling procedure and can affect uncertainty estimates. Spatial sample allocation should remain distinct from importance sampling over path or event space. Prerequisites
Sampling aliasing and reconstruction — Allocation/filtering must respect what reduced samples can distinguish. Multiscale texture filtering — Coarse samples need appropriate prefilter/footprint representations. Appendix.title: Cross-volume companion reference
Appendix.Content:
This companion appears in Volume 2, The Foundations Bible — Volume II: Numerical Methods, Probability, Geometry and Camera Systems: Reflection refraction and shading directions — Reflection refraction and shading directions Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: Phase6 · Latest development: University courses Definition and mechanism Plane reflection reverses a direction’s normal component. Refraction scales its tangent component by the incident/transmitted index ratio and solves for a unit normal component. A negative computed discriminant indicates total internal reflection under the stated model. Half-vectors require normalized outward light/view directions. Incident <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mn>0.6</mn> <mo>,</mo> <mn>0</mn> <mo>,</mo> <mo>−</mo> <mn>0.8</mn> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </math> reflects to <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mn>0.6</mn> <mo>,</mo> <mn>0</mn> <mo>,</mo> <mn>0.8</mn> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </math> across normal <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mn>0</mn> <mo>,</mo> <mn>0</mn> <mo>,</mo> <mn>1</mn> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </math>. Antiparallel light/view directions have no unique half-vector. Prerequisites
Projection rejection and scalar components — Removing an unwanted component creates residuals, tangent axes and mirror decompositions. Unit directions and safe normalization — Validated finite unit directions establish the preconditions for simplified geometry formulas.
Used by Later curriculum sources can deepen this same node; no future coverage is marked complete. - Lens optics and depth of field Recall and next depth Declare arrow and medium conventions before deriving formulas; distinguish direction geometry from optical energy. Full production proofs, target-specific integration and learner mastery require further evidence. Source and navigation Teaching narrative · Coverage and source gap · Evidence and limits · Dependency Map University course development Extend the existing direction note by separating geometric surface orientation from optical ray behavior. The normal vector is perpendicular to a local tangent plane; it determines the cosine term in diffuse shading and the directions of ideal reflection and refraction. For unit incident direction <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <msub> <mi>ω</mi> <mi>i</mi> </msub> </math> and unit normal <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>n</mi> </math>, specular reflection mirrors the direction about the normal, while refraction changes direction according to the ratio of refractive indices and may undergo total internal reflection. Direction conventions matter: some texts define incoming vectors toward the surface, others point away from it, so signs must be checked before applying formulas. A shading normal may differ from the true geometric normal, as in normal mapping, but it cannot change silhouette or visibility. Distinguish shading perturbations from geometry displacement, and use consistent normals when evaluating BRDFs, ray offsets, and medium transitions. Lens optics, focus, and image formation · Reflectance, BRDFs, and shading · Shape from shading and reflectance. Open Reflection refraction and shading directions in Volume 2

Appendix.title: Cross-volume companion reference
Appendix.Content:
This companion appears in Volume 2, The Visual Computing Bible — Volume II: Computational Geometry, Vision, Reconstruction and XR: Learned image features and CNNs — Learned image features and CNNs Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: University courses · Latest development: University courses Definition and mechanism A convolutional neural network (CNN) learns filters that detect useful image patterns from data. A convolution layer applies the same small kernel at many image locations, so a feature such as an edge can be recognized wherever it appears. Early layers often respond to local contrast or texture; later layers combine these responses into task-specific patterns. Stride and pooling reduce spatial resolution, trading detail for computation and larger receptive fields. Training adjusts filter values by gradient descent using backpropagation and labeled or self-supervised objectives. Weight sharing gives translation equivariance: shifting an input shifts the feature map, but does not guarantee full translation invariance or robustness to scale, viewpoint, lighting, or distribution change. Padding and stride determine border behavior and output size; too much downsampling can erase small objects. A learned feature is a representation useful for a training objective, not a human-interpretable semantic guarantee. Performance depends on data coverage, augmentation, architecture, optimization, and honest held-out evaluation. Prerequisites
Convolution and filter footprints Sampling aliasing and reconstruction Research validity and ablation Retinal encoding and receptive fields Automatic differentiation and backpropagation
Used by
Convolutional models preserve image neighborhoods Attention and visual transformers Contrastive vision and image-language alignment Perception feedback and robot learning

M004 - Representation and rounding learning spine Prerequisites Dependent Why these steps are needed IEEE-754 floating point, Bit field Binary32 A 32-bit binary interchange format with one sign bit, eight exponent bits and 23 fraction bits. Normal precision is 24 bits; exponent bias is 127. Word 3F800000 has E=127,F=0 and means 1. Binary32 Binary64 A 64-bit binary interchange format with 1/11/52 fields, 53 significant normal bits and bias 1023. Normal exponent range is −1022 through 1023. Word 3FF0000000000000 means 1. Binary32 Exponent bias Normal exponents are encoded as unsigned E=e+B. Binary32 B=127, so exponent 3 stores 130. Field zero and all-ones are reserved; classify before subtracting bias. Binary32, Positional notation Significand and hidden bit The significand supplies significant digits; the exponent supplies scale. A normal binary value begins 1.f, so its leading one is implied, not stored. Binary32 fraction F contributes F/2^23; subnormals instead begin 0.f. Exponent bias, Significand and hidden bit, Hexadecimal Floating-point encoding and decoding Encoding chooses fields for a value; decoding classifies fields and reconstructs their meaning. 10.625 normalizes to 1.010101₂×2³, giving 412A0000. C1540000 decodes to −13.25. Binary32 Signed zero Exponent and fraction zero permit either sign. 00000000 and 80000000 compare numerically equal, but signbit and reciprocal distinguish them. Ordinary x<0 does not detect negative zero. Binary32 Floating-point infinities All-one exponent and zero fraction encode signed infinity. This is not maximum finite. Infinity minus itself is NaN; overflow’s result also depends on rounding direction. Binary32 NaNs and payloads All-one exponent with nonzero fraction encodes a non-numerical, unordered NaN. Quiet and signaling classes differ; fraction bits can carry payload information. Ordinary NaN equality is false; use isnan. Raw words can be classified without consuming signaling NaNs as floating values. Exponent bias, Significand and hidden bit Subnormals and gradual underflow Exponent zero and nonzero fraction remove the hidden one and hold the effective exponent at the normal minimum. Binary32 values are F×2^-149, connecting smoothly to 2^-126. Absolute spacing stays fixed while relative precision degrades. Significand and hidden bit Machine epsilon For these binary types epsilon is upward spacing at 1: 2^-23 for binary32 and 2^-52 for binary64. It is neither minimum positive value nor a physical threshold. Machine epsilon, Exponent bias, Subnormals and gradual underflow ULP and representable spacing A unit in the last place describes local spacing. Inside normal binade [2e,2(e+1)), p-bit precision gives spacing 2^(e-(p-1)). Immediately above 1 the binary32 gap is twice the gap below it. ULP and representable spacing Rounding to nearest ties to even Choose the nearest representable value; exactly halfway choose the even retained significand integer. At toy precision three bits, 1.125→1 and 1.375→1.5. std::round uses halfway-away-from-zero instead. ULP and representable spacing, Rounding to nearest ties to even Unit roundoff Under nearest binary rounding the conventional relative bound for normal-range results is u=2^-p, half upward epsilon. For binary32 this is 2^-24. The bound has range/rounding assumptions. Boolean algebra, Rounding to nearest ties to even Guard round and sticky bits Guard is first discarded bit, round the next, sticky ORs all remaining bits. With retained low bit L, nearest-even increments when G AND (R OR sticky OR L). Sticky summarizes any nonzero tail. Rounding to nearest ties to even Directed rounding modes Upward means toward positive infinity, downward toward negative infinity, and toward-zero truncates magnitude. Upward rounding of −2.1 to an integer gives −2, not −3. Directed rounding modes, NaNs and payloads Floating-point environment and compiler modes The environment includes rounding direction and exception status. Runtime mode changes can fail and must restore prior state. Strict compiler settings are needed; fast-math may discard required special-value or environment assumptions. IEEE-754 floating point, Subnormals and gradual underflow Floating-point exception flags Invalid, divide-by-zero, overflow, underflow and inexact are status conditions, not C++ throw exceptions. Exact subnormal results need not signal underflow. Flag/trap behavior depends on the environment. Subnormals and gradual underflow, Floating-point environment and compiler modes Flush-to-zero and denormals-are-zero FTZ flushes certain tiny results to zero; DAZ treats subnormal inputs as zero in supporting environments. They change gradual-underflow behavior. Cost and support are target/mode-specific. Fixed-width integer types, Interpretation contract, IEEE-754 floating point Bit casting and representation A same-size eligible bit_cast transfers representation, not numeric value. On the checked binary32 host, bit_cast<uint32_t>(1.0f)=3F800000, whereas a numeric cast gives 1. Pointer punning is not an equivalent legal operation. ULP and representable spacing, Signed zero, NaNs and payloads ULP distance policies Distance counts representable steps under a declared ordering/equality policy. The finite-only laboratory collapses both zeros to one key and rejects NaNs/infinities. Across negative minimum subnormal to positive minimum subnormal distance is two. Machine epsilon, ULP and representable spacing, Floating-point infinities, NaNs and payloads Numerical tolerance policies Tolerance is a task-chosen allowed discrepancy: absolute in original units, relative to scale, or representable-step based. Machine epsilon is not automatically a norm cutoff. Handle non-finite values and validate tolerances before formulas. IEEE-754 floating point, Floating-point infinities Robust norm and intermediate range A final representable answer can be lost to overflowing intermediates. Squaring 1e20f overflows before a finite norm could be formed. Scale by maximum component or use hypot to avoid unnecessary squared overflow. Numerical tolerance policies Conditioning and singularity Conditioning measures sensitivity to input perturbation. A=1e-4 I has determinant 1e-8 but condition number one in the 2-norm. Uniform scaling changes determinant magnitude without changing this conditioning measure. Signed zero, NaNs and payloads, Serialization, Bit casting and representation Floating-point canonicalization Canonicalization deliberately merges encodings: both zeros to positive zero, all NaNs to one quiet pattern. Raw preservation instead keeps sign/payload distinctions. Neither is universally correct; this is a file/hash contract choice. Directed rounding modes, Floating-point environment and compiler modes Interval arithmetic An interval encloses a possible exact value between lower and upper bounds. Correct outward rounding can preserve containment when the whole algorithm honors necessary assumptions. The first volume covers all Parts 1–100. Prerequisites explain the story’s dependencies; they do not require leaving the continuous volume to learn an essential definition. Representation choices and external contracts Prerequisites Dependent Why these steps are needed Two's complement, Interpretation contract Fixed-point representation A raw integer I represents I/S for an agreed positive scale S and units. With S=2^16, raw 212992 means 3.25. The integer has no built-in fractional point. Fixed-point representation Fixed-point range and resolution For signed N-bit raw storage and F fraction bits, step is 2^-F and the positive endpoint is (2(N-1)-1)/2F. Required step 0.001 and magnitude 1e6 in 32 bits allow F=10 or 11. Fixed-point representation, Minimum signed value, Arithmetic policies Fixed-point rescaling Raw multiplication changes scale S to S²; divide the wide product by S with a declared rounding rule. Raw division uses A*S/B. Check the destination after widening, and handle divisor zero and signed minima. Fixed-point representation, Absolute and relative error Affine quantization and zero point A positive step s, integer zero point z and bounded code q reconstruct x̂=s(q-z). Nearest encode uses clamp(round(x/s)+z). Half-step error assumes no clipping and ideal parameters. Affine quantization and zero point, Bit packing Groupwise quantization and metadata Local groups share a scale, improving adaptation at a metadata cost. Symmetric INT4 calibration maxAbs/7 reconstructs codes around [-7,7]; float scales add about 32/G bits per value for full groups. Quantization and compressed weights One-bit centroid quantization One sign label selects one of two row means. Row [-1,-3,2,4] reconstructs [-2,-2,3,3], with RMSE one. Two float32 centroids cost 64 additional bits per row. Affine quantization and zero point UNORM and SNORM UNORM decodes q/(2^n-1); UNORM8 code128 gives128/255. SNORM commonly clamps q/(2^(n-1)-1) at -1, so -128 and -127 both map to -1 for eight bits. IEEE-754 floating point, Rounding to nearest ties to even Binary16 IEEE binary16 has 1/5/10 fields, bias15 and11 normal precision bits. Word3E00 is1.5; maximum finite65504; normal minimum2^-14 and subnormal minimum2^-24. IEEE-754 floating point, Rounding to nearest ties to even Bfloat16 BF16 has1/8/7 fields, bias127 and8 normal precision bits. It keeps broad exponent range at coarse spacing2^-7 above1. A nearest-even conversion must handle NaNs separately from finite rounding. Unsigned modular arithmetic, Interpretation contract Offset-binary coding A bias turns signed levels into unsigned codes. For the source-shaped INT4 convention c=q+8, -3 becomes nibble0101, not the two’s-complement nibble1101. Absolute and relative error, Quantization and compressed weights Quantization error metrics For N>0, RMSE is sqrt(sum squared discrepancies/N), MAE is mean absolute discrepancy, and max error is the largest observed magnitude. Promote float operands before subtraction when measuring in double. Serialization, Bit casting and representation Binary format contracts A schema declares field widths/order, byte order, numeric representation, valid values, lengths, version, padding and identity policy. Magic identifies a candidate format; version chooses a schema, neither authenticates content. Binary format contracts, Unsigned modular arithmetic, Short-circuit evaluation Checked binary parsing Validate products before size calculation, ranges with offset≤size and length≤size-offset, and practical resource limits before allocation. Mapping/alignment does not itself establish valid typed object access. Bitwise XOR, Serialization Checksums CRCs and hashes Checksums/digests summarize specified bytes. Additive checksums miss reorderings; CRCs use GF(2) polynomial remainders and declared parameters. Cryptographic hashes need a trusted reference to support integrity claims against substitution. Checksums CRCs and hashes, Interpretation contract Integrity and authenticity Integrity compares content with a declared reference; authenticity requires a trust mechanism such as a MAC or signature. Replacing both file and untrusted digest defeats a simple hash comparison. Endianness, Bit casting and representation, Binary format contracts Memory dump interpretation Raw octets gain meaning from offsets, width, encoding and byte order. Bytes00 00 80 3F mean integer1065353216 or binary32 one under different little-endian contracts. A dump does not prove a typed object is live. This companion appears in Volume 2, The Foundations Bible — Volume II: Numerical Methods, Probability, Geometry and Camera Systems: Random variables and probability laws — Random variables and probability laws Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: Phase 10 · Latest development: Phase 10 Definition and mechanism A random variable is a measurable mapping from outcomes to numerical values; its probability law describes how those values are distributed. Discrete laws assign probability mass to points, while continuous laws use densities relative to a chosen measure. A cumulative distribution function exists for either kind and records probability accumulated up to a threshold. Mixed distributions can contain both atoms and continuous parts. Density is not probability at an exact point, and it changes with coordinates according to a Jacobian. Expectation integrates a function against the law, whether the variable is represented by a PMF or PDF. These distinctions matter in sampling APIs: returned value, support, endpoint behavior, and reported density must refer to the same measure. A finite computer sampler approximates a continuous law with finitely many representable outputs. Prerequisites
Probability spaces, events, and conditioning
Used by
Common probability distributions and their assumptions Expectation, covariance, and dependence Inverse, rejection, and importance sampling Probability density and change of measure

This companion appears in Volume 1, The Foundations Bible — Volume I: From Bits to Computation, C++, Memory and Systems: Multilevel pointer qualification — Multilevel pointer qualification Curriculum depth: Introduced · First seen: C008 · Latest development: C008 Definition and mechanism int** cannot implicitly become const int**: that would permit injection of an actually const object’s address into an original int*. int** can become const int* const*, whose intermediate read-only pointer blocks that assignment. Prerequisites
Const qualification and shallow constness — Access-path qualification constrains nested conversions and member writes.
Used by Later sources will deepen this same node; no empty dependent nodes are created. Recall and next depth Rebuild the hypothetical pointer injection step by step. Pending: qualification decomposition at further levels. Written coverage does not establish learner mastery. Source and navigation Teaching explanation and examples · Exact coverage · Dependency Map Const applies at each indirection level For a pointer chain, qualification is attached to a particular level rather than to the whole expression. const T* means the pointed-to T is not writable through that path; T* const means the pointer object itself cannot be reseated; const T* const combines both. The distinction becomes safety-critical at multiple levels. Converting T** to const T** is not generally safe: if it were allowed, code could store a pointer-to-const object into the outer pointer and later write through the original T*, violating const protection. Qualification conversions therefore follow stricter rules than the familiar T* -> const T* case. Engine APIs should avoid raw multi-level pointer mutation unless the ownership/indirection contract truly requires it. Spans, references to containers, output wrappers or typed handle arrays often express the real intent more clearly. A reconstruction exercise should explain each const position and demonstrate the classic unsafe hypothetical conversion.. Open Multilevel pointer qualification in Volume 1

This companion appears in Volume 2, The Visual Computing Bible — Volume II: Computational Geometry, Vision, Reconstruction and XR: Template matching and distance transforms — Template matching and distance transforms Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: University courses · Latest development: University courses Definition and mechanism Template matching searches an image for a known pattern by comparing a small reference patch at candidate positions. Sum of squared differences penalizes intensity mismatch; normalized correlation compensates for brightness scale and offset. Direct search costs work proportional to image area times template area, while convolution or Fourier methods can accelerate broad searches. Rotation and scale changes require transforming the template or searching additional parameters. For contour-based matching, a distance transform stores each pixel’s distance to the nearest edge. A template edge point then receives a low cost when it lands near an observed contour even if the exact pixels do not align. The chamfer score sums these distances over template points. These methods suit industrial inspection where the target geometry is known, but need explicit thresholds for occlusion, deformation, and false positives. Prerequisites
Convolution and filter footprints Edge localization and subpixel contours
Used by

This companion appears in Volume 2, The Visual Computing Bible — Volume II: Computational Geometry, Vision, Reconstruction and XR: Sampling aliasing and reconstruction — Sampling aliasing and reconstruction Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: XR01 · Latest development: Phase 10 Definition and mechanism Uniform samples identify frequencies only modulo sample rate and corresponding real-signal equivalences. Strictly band-limited ideal reconstruction needs non-overlapping spectral replicas; exact-Nyquist phase is a boundary hazard. Prefilter before decimation. Phase 9–10 development Signal aliasing occurs when distinct signal frequencies produce the same sampled values; reconstruction then cannot recover which signal generated the samples without additional assumptions. Stratification, low-discrepancy sequences, and blue-noise point sets describe where samples are placed, not a guarantee that the signal is band-limited or that an estimator is unbiased. Each strategy still needs a valid support, probability weight, and reconstruction filter. Prerequisites
Fourier analysis and spectral phase — Frequency and phase reveal transfer, sampling ambiguity and structural loss.
Used by
Multiscale texture filtering Spatiotemporal sampling and retinal motion Antialiasing and sample allocation Triangle rasterization and coverage tests Edge localization and subpixel contours PDE fields and discrete Laplacians Learned image features and CNNs Radiance fields and Gaussian splatting Reservoir resampling and ReSTIR Sampling quality: stratification, quasi-Monte Carlo, and blue noise Tensor-product interpolation ## Recall and next depth
Prove 13Hz and 3Hz sample identity at 10Hz. Pending: anisotropic/nonuniform sampling and actual reconstruction errors. Written coverage is not a claim of learner mastery or accepted numbered-curriculum progress. Source and navigation Expanded teaching explanation · Independent coverage · Dependency Map University course development Sampling records measurements of a continuous signal on a discrete grid. Frequencies that differ by integer multiples of the sampling rate can produce the same samples, so the sampled values alone cannot identify which original signal was present. For ideal band-limited reconstruction, the signal must be restricted below half the sampling rate; equality at the limiting frequency needs additional phase and endpoint conditions. A real pixel also integrates light over area and exposure time, making its measurement a filtered sample. Prefiltering attenuates frequencies that would alias, while reconstruction estimates a continuous signal from the stored samples. Ideal sinc reconstruction has infinite support; practical filters trade computation, sharpness, ringing and residual aliasing. More samples reduce integration error only when their placement and weights match the intended pixel or path-space measure. This companion appears in Volume 1, The Foundations Bible — Volume I: From Bits to Computation, C++, Memory and Systems: Shader buffer ABI — Shader buffer ABI A shader buffer is a binary interface between independently compiled code. CPU and shader code must agree on member offsets, element widths, alignment, array stride, matrix layout, and total record stride. “These structs have the same fields” is not enough. Suppose a record logically contains a 3-vector followed by a scalar. The mathematical payload is four floats, but the ABI may impose an alignment boundary for the vector or the containing record. The only safe statement is the one established by the layout rules and, ideally, reflection/compiled shader metadata. Layout is a function of context Different interfaces can have different rules: vertex attributes, constant/uniform buffers, storage buffers, argument buffers and push/root constants are not interchangeable contracts. Matrix row/column-major convention is another independent dimension. On the CPU side, standard C++ object layout also has rules about padding and alignment. Copying bytes from a native struct into a shader buffer is valid only when the native representation is deliberately made compatible or explicit serialization writes the expected offsets. Verify rather than guess A robust pipeline should generate or reflect a machine-readable layout description and compare it with CPU declarations:
expected offset for every member; expected array stride; matrix stride and orientation; record size/alignment; scalar widths and signedness.
Static assertions can catch CPU layout changes. Shader reflection or compiler metadata catches shader-side changes. A golden byte dump can test the complete bridge. Failure modes Common failures include using a 12-byte mental model for a vector type whose ABI slot is 16 bytes, mixing bool widths, assuming packed enums, copying pointer-containing structs, row/column-major disagreement, and updating one side of the interface without rebuilding the other. Teach and reconstruct: Continuous Notes/Computing Foundations - From Bits to C++ and Systems APIs#Make a shader record an explicit binary contract. Related: Alignment and padding, GPU vertex specification, Tensor runtime layout and views.. Open Shader buffer ABI in Volume 1

This companion appears in Volume 2, The Visual Computing Bible — Volume II: Computational Geometry, Vision, Reconstruction and XR: GPU vertex specification — GPU vertex specification Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: University courses · Latest development: University courses Definition and mechanism A GPU vertex-input specification explains how bytes in one or more buffers become per-vertex shader inputs. A buffer object owns bytes; a vertex array object records their interpretation: enabled attributes, component count and type, normalization, stride, byte offset, and the buffer binding used for fetch. Stride is the number of bytes between successive vertices; offset is the first component’s byte position. For vertex i, the address is base + offset + i × stride. For interleaved records containing position (3 floats), normal (3), and UV (2), the stride is 8 × 4 = 32 bytes and the UV offset is 24 bytes. Modern binding APIs separate attribute format from the buffer binding; older pointer-style calls can capture the buffer bound at setup time. A wrong stride may still address valid memory, so the symptom is often plausible but scrambled geometry. The contract must agree with CPU packing, shader input types, and the API’s state-capture rules. Prerequisites
Vector storage SIMD and boundary layouts Matrix storage indexing and strides Camera view and clip-space pipeline Pointer arithmetic and provenance
Used by

This companion appears in Volume 2, The Visual Computing Bible — Volume II: Computational Geometry, Vision, Reconstruction and XR: Contrastive vision and image-language alignment — Contrastive vision and image-language alignment Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: University courses · Latest development: University courses Definition and mechanism Contrastive image-language learning trains an image encoder and a text encoder to place matching descriptions near their images in a shared feature space. For a batch of paired examples, cosine similarities between normalized embeddings form a score matrix; a temperature scales the scores, and an InfoNCE-style cross-entropy treats the matching pair as the positive while other batch items act as negatives. The objective makes retrieval and zero-shot label comparison possible by encoding class names as text. It learns statistical alignment, not a guarantee that every phrase is grounded in the pixels. Batch composition, duplicate or semantically similar negatives, captions, and web-data biases all shape the representation. A model may associate a prompt with correlated context rather than the requested object, and similarity scores are not calibrated probabilities. Evaluation must distinguish retrieval, classification, localization, and reasoning rather than treating one score as general visual understanding. Prerequisites

This companion appears in Volume 1, The Foundations Bible — Volume I: From Bits to Computation, C++, Memory and Systems: TLB — TLB Curriculum depth: Introduced · First seen: C003 · Latest development: C003 Definition and mechanism The translation lookaside buffer caches recent address translations and relevant access metadata, not the bytes being loaded. A miss may trigger a valid page-table walk without OS fault handling. A TLB hit can coexist with a data-cache miss. Context and permissions matter; it is not just a global VPN-only dictionary. Prerequisites

Used by

Recall and next depth Distinguish a translation miss, cache miss, and page fault. Pending: ASIDs/PCIDs, shootdowns, hierarchy, associativity, and measured reach. Source and navigation C003 teaching chapter · Part definitions · Dependency Map Reconstruction depth The Translation Lookaside Buffer caches recent virtual-page to physical-frame translations. Without a cached translation, the processor performs a page-table walk, which itself requires memory accesses and can stall an otherwise cache-friendly loop. TLB locality differs from data-cache locality. A traversal can touch one cache line from thousands of separate pages: each useful access is small, but the page working set can exceed TLB capacity. Huge pages increase TLB reach because one translation covers more bytes, although they introduce allocation and fragmentation trade-offs. When profiling, do not diagnose every unexplained memory stall as a TLB problem. Hardware performance counters can separate cache misses, page walks and TLB misses on supported CPUs. Synthetic experiments should vary stride and working-set pages while keeping useful work controlled. For engine data, dense arrays often help both cache and TLB locality; pointer-heavy structures can hurt both. NUMA adds another axis: a translation may be cached while the physical page still resides on a remote node.. Open TLB in Volume 1

This companion appears in Volume 2, The Foundations Bible — Volume II: Numerical Methods, Probability, Geometry and Camera Systems: Derivative as a local linear map — Derivative as a local linear map Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: Phase 9 · Latest development: Phase 9 Definition and mechanism The derivative measures first-order change. In one variable it is the limit of the difference quotient; in several variables it is the linear map that best predicts small output changes near a point. For a scalar function, this local model is the tangent line. For a vector-valued function, it is a matrix acting on an input perturbation. The derivative is local: its approximation error becomes small relative to the perturbation as the step shrinks, but the linear model need not remain accurate over a large region. This view unifies instantaneous velocity, gradients, Jacobians, and optimization directions. It also gives a practical check: compare a small finite perturbation with the derivative’s predicted change, while remembering that floating-point rounding and curvature limit how small or large the perturbation should be. This companion appears in Volume 2, The Foundations Bible — Volume II: Numerical Methods, Probability, Geometry and Camera Systems: Implicit differentiation and parameter sensitivities — Implicit differentiation and parameter sensitivities Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: Phase 9 · Latest development: Phase 9 Definition and mechanism Implicit differentiation obtains how a solution changes when it is defined by an equation rather than an explicit formula. If a state satisfies F(y,θ)=0 and the Jacobian with respect to y is invertible, differentiating gives dy/dθ=−(∂F/∂y)⁻¹(∂F/∂θ). This can differentiate equilibrium states, constrained optima, and roots without unrolling every solver iteration. For a converged optimizer, differentiating stationarity and constraint conditions yields sensitivity equations, but active-set changes, nonunique solutions, singular Jacobians, and imperfect convergence complicate the result. Continuous sensitivity equations propagate derivatives alongside an ODE; adjoint methods can reduce cost when there are many parameters and few scalar outputs. These are modeling tools with assumptions, not a guarantee that every algorithmic branch is differentiable. Prerequisites
Automatic differentiation and backpropagation Constrained optimization and inverse kinematics ODE integration and stability

This companion appears in Volume 2, The Foundations Bible — Volume II: Numerical Methods, Probability, Geometry and Camera Systems: Ray differentials and camera sampling measures — Ray differentials and camera sampling measures Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: Phase 11 Definition and mechanism A camera sample selects a film location and usually a shutter time, then maps that sample to a weighted ray or path contribution. Ray differentials approximate how neighboring pixel samples change the generated ray; after intersection they estimate the surface footprint covered by a pixel and help choose a texture filter level. A sampling measure states which quantity is sampled and therefore which probability density belongs in a Monte Carlo estimator; area, solid angle, image-plane area, and discrete pixel measures are not interchangeable without a Jacobian. Example: two adjacent pixels generate rays whose intersection points span a large patch on a distant oblique surface, so filtering should average that footprint rather than use a single high-frequency texel. Differential rays are local first-order approximations and can fail at discontinuities or complex lens mappings; the weight and PDF must match the camera model and chosen measure. Example: For a pinhole camera, offset the raster sample by one pixel in x and y, generate neighboring rays, and intersect them with a textured plane; the resulting parallelogram estimates the pixel footprint for texture filtering. Assumptions: Differentials approximate nearby rays locally and are not exact at visibility or lens discontinuities.; Importance weights/PDFs are valid only when defined in the same measure as the estimator. Prerequisites
Camera view and clip-space pipeline Visual angle and calibrated rays Lens optics and depth of field
Used by

This companion appears in Volume 2, The Foundations Bible — Volume II: Numerical Methods, Probability, Geometry and Camera Systems: Inverse, rejection, and importance sampling — Inverse, rejection, and importance sampling Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: Phase 10 · Latest development: Phase 10 Definition and mechanism Sampling transforms convert simpler random inputs into a target law. Inverse-CDF sampling maps a uniform value through a quantile function; rejection sampling accepts proposal draws according to a bounded target-to-proposal ratio; importance sampling estimates an integral by dividing each sampled integrand by the actual proposal density. Each method requires correct support and endpoint handling. Importance sampling is unbiased when the proposal covers every contributing region and the weighted contribution is integrable; finite variance additionally requires the integral of f²/p to be finite. Rejection sampling needs a valid finite envelope. Discrete floating-point inputs can hit boundaries that have zero probability in an ideal continuous model. Report the density with its measure and use the same measure in the estimator. A proposal that misses target support cannot be repaired by a larger weight. Prerequisites
Random variables and probability laws Probability density and change of measure Stateful pseudorandom generators and stream state

This companion appears in Volume 1, The Foundations Bible — Volume I: From Bits to Computation, C++, Memory and Systems: Quaternion rotation and double cover — Quaternion rotation and double cover Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: Phase7 · Latest development: University courses Definition and mechanism For a unit quaternion q, the sandwich q(0,v)conjugate(q) rotates v. q and minus q give the same physical rotation. Every nonzero quaternion also rotates without scale if its true inverse is used; substituting conjugate for inverse off the unit sphere scales by the squared norm. Reconstruction cue: The scalar-first quaternion (sqrt(1/2),0,0,sqrt(1/2)) rotates the X axis to Y. Prerequisites
Quaternion algebra and Hamilton product
Used by
Quaternion matrix and axis-angle conversion Quaternion interpolation and shortest paths

Deeper algorithms and measured production performance remain separate from the present model. Source and navigation Continuous explanation · Coverage and source gap · Sources and verification University course development Extend the existing quaternion note with interpolation and sign handling in animation. A unit quaternion represents a 3D rotation, but <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>q</mi> </math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mo>−</mo> <mi>q</mi> </math> encode the same physical orientation. If two endpoint quaternions have a negative dot product, negate one endpoint before interpolation so the path follows the shorter arc on the unit four-dimensional sphere. Linear interpolation followed by normalization is inexpensive and often adequate for close orientations; spherical linear interpolation travels at constant angular speed for widely separated rotations. Quaternion interpolation acts on orientation, while translation and scale need their own rules. This matters in camera paths and articulated characters: interpolating four components without handling the double cover can create an unnecessary long spin, while interpolating Euler angles can encounter a gimbal singularity. Validate unit length after operations subject to floating-point drift. Coordinate frames, transformations, and pose · Scene graphs and articulated geometry · Animation curves and motion paths. This companion appears in Volume 1, The Foundations Bible — Volume I: From Bits to Computation, C++, Memory and Systems: Serialization — Serialization Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: C001 · Latest development: C006 Definition and mechanism Serialization maps semantic fields to a specified byte sequence; decoding validates and reconstructs them. Width, order, version, bounds, and padding policy belong to that contract. A U8/U32-LE/U64-LE header occupies 13 bytes at offsets 0/1/5, independently of a native record’s possible 16-byte ABI layout. Packing removes some holes, not host dependencies. Publication and durability are subsequent operations. M004 extension: a binary32 representation word such as 3F800000 can be serialized as little-endian bytes 00 00 80 3F. Raw-bit preservation retains signed-zero and NaN-payload differences; canonicalization deliberately merges them. Numeric equality does not imply byte identity. This is a format policy, not permission to change existing files. M006 adds explicit schema/version/identity contracts, overflow-safe dimensions and resource limits, raw-word payload preservation, integrity coverage and a complete 52-byte demonstration. A native scalar writer is not automatically cross-endian stable. Prerequisites
Interpretation contract — Representation, type, and lifetime must identify what object exists. Fixed-width integer types — The representation width fixes byte count and valid shift range. Endianness — Byte order tells how digit significance maps to sequence positions.
Used by
Binary format contracts — uses this mechanism to define its representation, error or validation contract. Checksums CRCs and hashes — uses this mechanism to define its representation, error or validation contract. Floating-point canonicalization — uses serialization to establish this mechanism’s representation or policy. Atomic publication and durability — uses this mechanism as stated in its prerequisites.

The surface rendering equation adds emission and cosine-weighted incoming contributions. Visibility and transport assumptions matter; blurring completed output does not avoid shading. Prerequisites
Light spectra and radiometry — The light quantity and units must be established before its interaction or visual effect is modeled.
Used by Later independent XR sources will extend this same node. - Monte Carlo rendering estimators and variance - Surface orientation from image brightness

Written coverage is not a claim of learner mastery or accepted numbered-curriculum progress. Source and navigation Expanded teaching explanation · Independent coverage · Dependency Map University course development Extend the existing light-transport note with the distinction between a material’s directional response and the incident illumination it receives. At surface point <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>x</mi> </math>, outgoing radiance depends on emitted radiance plus an integral over incoming directions. The BRDF <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <msub> <mi>f</mi> <mi>r</mi> </msub> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mi>x</mi> <mo>,</mo> <msub> <mi>ω</mi> <mi>i</mi> </msub> <mo>,</mo> <msub> <mi>ω</mi> <mi>o</mi> </msub> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </math> is reflected outgoing radiance per incident irradiance, with units of inverse steradians; it depends on incoming direction <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <msub> <mi>ω</mi> <mi>i</mi> </msub> </math> and viewing direction <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <msub> <mi>ω</mi> <mi>o</mi> </msub> </math>. A physically plausible BRDF is nonnegative and conserves energy, but can still have narrow glossy lobes that are difficult to sample. The rendering equation combines this local material response with visibility, incoming radiance, and the cosine foreshortening factor. This form explains why shading, direct lighting, global illumination, and Monte Carlo integration are connected parts of one transport calculation rather than independent image effects. This companion appears in Volume 1, The Foundations Bible — Volume I: From Bits to Computation, C++, Memory and Systems: Alignment and padding — Alignment and padding Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: C002 · Latest development: C003 Definition and mechanism Alignment A restricts valid object starts to addresses divisible by A. alignof reports type alignment, which need not equal sizeof; alignas requests a supported stronger alignment. Padding fills layout holes and rounds array stride. Under 1/4/1 member rules, byte–uint32–byte uses offsets 0/4/8 and size 12. Power-of-two masks test low bits; checked align-up avoids unsigned overflow. Prerequisites
Byte and octet — Byte units define both storage offsets and significance digits. Addresses and virtual memory — Mappings give numeric locations their process-specific storage identity.
Used by

Internal and tail padding — uses this mechanism as stated in its prerequisites. Packed structures and misaligned access — uses this mechanism as stated in its prerequisites. Dynamic allocation and heap — uses this mechanism as stated in its prerequisites. SIMD and GPU data layouts — depends on this concept; see its prerequisite explanation.

Appendix.title: Cross-volume companion reference
Appendix.Content:
This companion appears in Volume 2, The Visual Computing Bible — Volume II: Computational Geometry, Vision, Reconstruction and XR: Attention and visual transformers — Attention and visual transformers Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: University courses · Latest development: University courses Definition and mechanism Self-attention lets each token build a context-dependent mixture of other tokens. A learned linear map produces queries <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>Q</mi> </math>, keys <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>K</mi> </math>, and values <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>V</mi> </math>; scaled dot products compare each query with all keys, softmax converts scores to weights, and those weights combine values. Multiple heads learn different relationships, while positional information tells the model where patches or words came from. Vision transformers split an image into patches, embed them as tokens, and process the sequence with attention and feed-forward blocks. Unlike a small convolution, global attention can relate distant regions in one layer, but its pairwise score matrix grows roughly as the square of token count. Patch size trades spatial detail for compute; positional encodings and training data affect transfer. Attention weights are a mechanism for mixing information, not an explanation of causal importance. A transformer still needs a task objective, data, optimization, and validation, and can fail under distribution shift or poor spatial grounding. Prerequisites
Convolution and filter footprints Probability density and change of measure Research validity and ablation Automatic differentiation and backpropagation Learned image features and CNNs
Used by

Appendix.title: Cross-volume companion reference
Appendix.Content:
This companion appears in Volume 2, The Visual Computing Bible — Volume II: Computational Geometry, Vision, Reconstruction and XR: Color encoding and linear-light operations — Color encoding and linear-light operations Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: XR01 · Latest development: University courses Definition and mechanism Color primaries/white point and nonlinear transfer encoding are different. Physical intensity filtering uses the appropriate linear quantity; black/white averaging then sRGB encoding gives about 0.735, not encoded 0.5. Tone/gamut mapping and absolute display luminance need separate contracts. Prerequisites
Light spectra and radiometry — The light quantity and units must be established before its interaction or visual effect is modeled. Interpretation contract — A numeric sample requires a domain, units and encoding convention.
Used by
Perceptual metrics and display calibration Exposure and sensor response
Recall and next depth State the metric’s encoding and peak before comparing images. Pending: standardized HDR and measured display calibration. Written coverage is not a claim of learner mastery or accepted numbered-curriculum progress. Source and navigation Expanded teaching explanation · Independent coverage · Dependency Map University course development Extend the existing color note with why image-processing arithmetic must distinguish encoded values from light. A display encoding such as sRGB uses a nonlinear transfer curve so code values allocate precision in a way that suits perception and storage. Averaging or adding those encoded numbers does not generally average or add emitted light. Decode to linear-light RGB before blending, filtering, estimating radiance, or compositing, then encode for display. If two equal-area samples contain linear intensities <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mn>0</mn> </math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mn>1</mn> </math>, their physical average is <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mn>0.5</mn> </math>; averaging their encoded sRGB values and treating that result as light yields a different, brighter answer. Color primaries and a white point also define the coordinate system of RGB, so a numeric triplet is incomplete without its color space. Keep scene-referred radiance, display-referred color, and perceptual appearance separate. Color perception, encoding, and display · Light measurement and radiometry · Image sampling, filtering, and efficient reconstruction. Open Color encoding and linear-light operations in Volume 2

This companion appears in Volume 1, The Foundations Bible — Volume I: From Bits to Computation, C++, Memory and Systems: Borrow contracts and pool epochs — Borrow contracts and pool epochs Curriculum depth: Introduced · First seen: C008 · Latest development: C008 Definition and mechanism An epoch versions a borrow-validity interval. A checked borrow compares its saved epoch to the live pool counter before using the cached element. The pool counter must outlive the borrow; counters alone do not supply ownership, synchronization, race freedom or wrap immunity. Prerequisites
Borrow invalidation and logical identity — Invalidating mutations define the deadlines a saved epoch or deferred borrow must respect.

Its entries sum A(i,k)B(k,j) over the shared dimension. Composition is associative over exact scalars and usually noncommutative; floating-point evaluation orders need not agree bitwise. Reconstruction cue: Rotation followed by translation differs from translation followed by rotation. Prerequisites

Optimization path figures: narrow quadratic valley and projected-bound optimum. Show Euclidean steepest direction changes under parameter scaling and why active-bound gradients need not vanish.
The six figure assets have been rendered as PNG and SVG files and embedded in the staged volume above. Final vault link resolution remains for the parent integration pass. Topic route
Functions and local change Jacobians and curvature Integration Simulation Automatic differentiation Optimization
Six figures
F09-1. Tangent prediction and local residual. At h=0.2, the exact residual for the shown exponential is about 0.03529 and the quadratic leading term about 0.03297; this illustrates local-order behavior.
F09-2. Accumulated area and the derivative that recovers the integrand. For A(x)=x cubed/3 at x=1.8, A=1.944 and A prime=3.24=x squared.
F09-3. Quadrature error as sample intervals increase. For exp(x) on [0,1] at N=16, left-rule error is about 0.053137, trapezoid error 5.593e-4, and Simpson error 1.456e-7; Simpson uses an even interval count.
F09-4. Energy behavior for the stated harmonic-oscillator step size. At h=0.1 for 80 periods, explicit Euler energy reaches about 2.62e21, semi-implicit Euler stays in [0.47619,0.526316], and RK4 ends near 0.499965. This is the plotted setup, not a universal ranking.
F09-5. Full Newton step versus Armijo backtracking for the plotted log-cosh example. At x=3, the full step is about -100.8566; backtracking first accepts alpha=0.03125 in this setup.
F09-6. Central-difference truncation and roundoff for sin(x) at x=0.7. The analytic derivative is cos(0.7), about 0.7648422; the best sampled step has error about 8.94e-13. This companion appears in Volume 2, The Visual Computing Bible — Volume II: Computational Geometry, Vision, Reconstruction and XR: Perception feedback and robot learning — Perception feedback and robot learning Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: University courses · Latest development: University courses Definition and mechanism A robot learning system closes a loop: sensors produce observations, a policy chooses an action, the world changes, and new observations arrive. A policy maps states or observations to actions; a value function estimates expected future return and can help compare actions. Reinforcement learning updates behavior from outcomes, while imitation learning fits demonstrations. In visual robotics, the observation pipeline may include cameras, learned features, pose estimates, and spatial grounding; errors then affect movement rather than only a label. The training and deployment distributions can differ because the robot’s own actions change what it sees. Small perception errors can compound into different states and larger future errors, a form of covariate or distribution shift. Stable deployment therefore needs calibrated sensing, feedback timing, safety constraints, and evaluation on physical conditions. Demonstrations in simulation do not establish robust real-world manipulation; embodiment, contact, latency, and unmodeled dynamics matter. A successful policy is evidence for a task and setting, not general intelligence. Prerequisites

This companion appears in Volume 2, The Visual Computing Bible — Volume II: Computational Geometry, Vision, Reconstruction and XR: Fourier analysis and spectral phase — Fourier analysis and spectral phase Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: XR01 · Latest development: University courses Definition and mechanism Fourier coordinates encode frequency magnitude and phase; phase places structure. DFT analyzes a finite periodic block, FFT computes that transform efficiently, and finite-window leakage differs from bin spacing. Interior one-sided amplitude bins need conjugate-pair normalization. Prerequisites
Continuous signals and discrete samples — Filtering/frequency analysis operates on a declared domain and its samples.
Used by

Written coverage is not a claim of learner mastery or accepted numbered-curriculum progress. Source and navigation Expanded teaching explanation · Independent coverage · Dependency Map University course development Extend the existing frequency-domain treatment with visual interpretation and filtering consequences. A Fourier coefficient records how strongly a sinusoidal basis function occurs at a given frequency and phase. In images, the origin of a two-dimensional spectrum represents slow spatial variation; moving farther from it corresponds to finer variation. A broad bright center indicates low-frequency structure, while energy far from the center often represents edges and texture. Filtering multiplies each frequency by the filter response: a low-pass response suppresses fine detail, and a high-pass response emphasizes it. Aliasing folds unresolved high frequencies into lower ones because sampled sinusoids can share identical sample values. This explains moiré patterns and animated shimmer, and shows why a spectrum is useful for diagnosing sampling problems rather than only for theoretical signal processing. Sampling continuous signals and image formation · Image sampling, filtering, and efficient reconstruction · Edges, contours, and subpixel localization. This companion appears in Volume 2, The Foundations Bible — Volume II: Numerical Methods, Probability, Geometry and Camera Systems: Reproducible numerical benchmarking — Reproducible numerical benchmarking Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: Phase 10 · Latest development: Phase 10 Definition and mechanism A useful numerical benchmark separates sample-level variability from run-level variability and pairs competing methods on the same inputs or seeds. Record the algorithm, precision, compiler/runtime settings, sample count, seed or keyed input, warm-up policy, timing method, and error metric. Compare distributions or paired differences rather than a single favorable run. A speed improvement is meaningful only if accuracy and failure rates remain acceptable for the target workload. For Monte Carlo methods, repeat independent runs and report uncertainty; for deterministic solvers, use analytical or manufactured solutions and measure convergence. Reproducibility is an experimental contract, not merely a fixed random seed. If the workload is stochastic, compare paired seeds and report both runtime and error distributions. Prerequisites

This companion appears in Volume 2, The Visual Computing Bible — Volume II: Computational Geometry, Vision, Reconstruction and XR: Radiance fields and Gaussian splatting — Radiance fields and Gaussian splatting Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: University courses · Latest development: University courses Definition and mechanism A radiance field represents a scene by the color and density seen along each 3D viewing ray. NeRF maps a position and viewing direction through a learned function, then volume-renders samples using transmittance and opacity weights; multiple calibrated photographs supervise the result. This representation handles view-dependent appearance but can require many ray samples and careful camera alignment. 3D Gaussian splatting instead stores anisotropic colored Gaussian primitives in space and projects them to screen, sorting and blending their footprints for fast interactive views. 2D Gaussian splatting uses oriented surface-like splats to improve geometric consistency. These methods trade continuous function evaluation for explicit primitives and rasterization. Sparse or biased views leave unseen regions unconstrained; floaters, blur, aliasing, incorrect transparency ordering, or poor geometry can remain even when training views look convincing. Novel-view quality is not equivalent to a watertight mesh or physically correct material. Reconstruction quality depends on camera poses, coverage, calibration, and the scene’s changing illumination. This companion appears in Volume 2, The Foundations Bible — Volume II: Numerical Methods, Probability, Geometry and Camera Systems: Homogeneous coordinates and perspective division — Homogeneous coordinates and perspective division Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: Phase6 · Latest development: University courses Definition and mechanism Phase 7 derives the affine block matrix, distinguishes a singular affine map from an invertible frame, and traces model → view → homogeneous clip → NDC using a declared projection. The worked figure keeps the divisor visible and checks the chosen near/far depth endpoints. An affine homogeneous point has last coordinate one; a direction has zero. Nonzero common scale defines projective equivalence, while dehomogenization divides by a nonzero final component. Clip representatives and projective classes have related but distinct semantics. <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mn>2</mn> <mo>,</mo> <mn>4</mn> <mo>,</mo> <mn>6</mn> <mo>,</mo> <mn>2</mn> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mn>1</mn> <mo>,</mo> <mn>2</mn> <mo>,</mo> <mn>3</mn> <mo>,</mo> <mn>1</mn> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </math> describe one finite projective point. NDC normalization standardizes ranges, not vector length. Prerequisites
Vectors coordinates and affine points — Point, displacement and coordinate roles determine which geometric operations are meaningful.
Used by
Linear affine and projective transformations
Later curriculum sources can deepen this same node; no future coverage is marked complete. - Ray-triangle intersection - Camera calibration and bundle adjustment

Recall and next depth Explain why perspective division is nonlinear and why clipping must precede casual division. Full production proofs, target-specific integration and learner mastery require further evidence. Source and navigation Teaching narrative · Coverage and source gap · Evidence and limits · Dependency Map University course development Extend the existing account with the geometric reason for the final divide. A 3D point is stored as <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mi>x</mi> <mo>,</mo> <mi>y</mi> <mo>,</mo> <mi>z</mi> <mo>,</mo> <mn>1</mn> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </math>; after multiplying by a projective matrix it becomes <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mi>X</mi> <mo>,</mo> <mi>Y</mi> <mo>,</mo> <mi>Z</mi> <mo>,</mo> <mi>W</mi> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </math>. Dividing the first three components by <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>W</mi> </math> maps the homogeneous representative to ordinary coordinates. Any nonzero scalar multiple of a homogeneous vector represents the same point, which is why this division is meaningful. For a perspective camera, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>W</mi> </math> is chosen to depend on depth, so apparent size shrinks with distance. A direction has homogeneous coordinate zero and is not translated like a point. Projection matrices encode the camera frustum before division; afterward, a viewport transform scales and shifts normalized coordinates to pixels and commonly flips the vertical axis because image rows increase downward. Keep clipping before division to avoid unstable behavior around <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>W</mi> <mo>=</mo> <mn>0</mn> </math>. Coordinate frames, transformations, and pose · Cameras, projection, and calibration Phase 11 camera development Homogeneous image coordinates represent a ray up to nonzero scale; perspective division produces normalized image coordinates. Monocular reconstruction has a separate physical scale gauge: multiplying all scene points and camera translations by the same positive factor preserves projections. Do not confuse representational scale with unknown metric scale. A known object dimension, baseline, or depth measurement can anchor metres; normalizing a homogeneous vector cannot. This assumes calibrated perspective projection without an external scale prior. The distinction explains why a numerically precise reconstruction can still lack physical units. Appendix.title: Cross-volume companion reference
Appendix.Content:
This companion appears in Volume 1, The Foundations Bible — Volume I: From Bits to Computation, C++, Memory and Systems: 10 - Probability and Monte Carlo - Visual Recall — Probability and uncertainty — visual recall
Shortest route: start with a model of outcomes, then ask what distribution the computer actually sampled, how it weighted each sample, and what evidence supports the estimate. Reconstruct the chain (Ω, F, P) describes outcomes, measurable events, and their probabilities. A random variable maps outcomes into numbers; a random vector preserves their joint behavior. A PMF assigns point mass to discrete values; a PDF gives density relative to a stated measure; a CDF accumulates probability and exists even when no PDF does. Conditioning changes the information available. Independence means joint probability factors, not merely that events are disjoint. Bayes reverses the conditioning direction by multiplying likelihood by prior and normalizing over alternatives. Expectation is a probability-weighted center. Variance is mean squared spread. Covariance records coupled variation; correlation divides it by both standard deviations but only captures linear association. For a vector, covariance is symmetric PSD because aᵀΣa = Var(aᵀX) ≥ 0. Bernoulli describes one binary outcome; binomial counts IID Bernoulli successes. Uniform has constant density in its declared measure. Gaussian describes a quadratic-distance bell shape. Exponential waiting times are memoryless; Poisson counts belong to the corresponding constant-rate process. A multivariate Gaussian’s covariance sets ellipse/ellipsoid orientation and scale. The computational chain is: seed/state or keyed input → finite random bits → sample transform → actual PDF and measure → weighted contribution f(X)/p(X) → average → uncertainty/error report Every arrow carries assumptions. A wrong PDF or measure can bias the result. A low-variance estimator can still be biased. Correlated observations change the standard error. Confidence intervals do not repair a wrong expectation. Formula prompts Prompt Reconstruct Conditioning P(A|B)=P(A∩B)/P(B); chain rule multiplies successive conditional probabilities. Bayes P(H|E)=P(E|H)P(H)/ΣᵢP(E|Hᵢ)P(Hᵢ). Expected transform E[g(X)] = Σg(x)p(x) or ∫g(x)p(x)dx. Variance/covariance Var(X)=E[X²]−E[X]²; Cov(X,Y)=E[XY]−E[X]E[Y]. Linear propagation E[AX+b]=Aμ+b; Cov(AX+b)=AΣAᵀ; local nonlinear approximation uses JΣJᵀ. Importance estimate I=∫f dx=Eₚ[f(X)/p(X)]; average contributions and divide by the actual sampling density. Monte Carlo error IID finite-variance mean has Var(Ȳ)=σ²/N, SE=σ/√N; four times samples halves SE. Estimator quality MSE = variance + bias². Bessel/Welford Unbiased sample variance uses M₂/(n−1); update with δ=x−μ, μ←μ+δ/n, M₂←M₂+δ(x−μ). Error metrics MSE squares; RMSE returns original units; MAE uses absolute error; relative metrics fail or need policy near zero. Fast error checks
Does a density integrate to one in the stated coordinate measure? Is its unit inverse measure? Are the samples distributed according to the PDF used in the weight? Is a stated confidence interval fixed-sample, and are IID/normal or approximation assumptions plausible? Is covariance symmetric PSD? Does singular mean invalid, or valid but lower-rank? Are sample and population variance being confused? Is a single run being mistaken for evidence of variance reduction? Is a “Gaussian” a normalized probability model or merely a rendering kernel?
Targeted backlinks
stable numerics conditioning coordinate changes positive definiteness covariance eigenstructure

Source-provided recall and compact formula reference Supplied concise recall summary The mathematical core is the probability space <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mi mathvariant="normal">Ω</mi> <mo>,</mo> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"> <mi data-mjx-variant="-tex-calligraphic" mathvariant="script">F</mi> </mrow> <mo>,</mo> <mi>P</mi> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </math>, random variables defined on that space, and probability laws for their values. Conditional probability changes the reference information. Independence is a factorization property. PMFs assign masses to discrete values, while PDFs assign density relative to a measure. CDFs accumulate probability and exist for every real-valued random variable. Expected value describes the weighted centre. Variance describes squared spread. Covariance describes coupled spread. Correlation standardizes covariance but does not measure every form of dependence. Bernoulli models one binary trial. Binomial models the count of successes in independent identically distributed Bernoulli trials. Uniform models constant density over a region. Gaussian models a particular smooth bell-shaped distribution. Exponential models memoryless waiting times. Poisson models event counts under its defining assumptions. A multivariate Gaussian combines mean, covariance, and correlations into a joint distribution. Positive-definite covariance permits a full-dimensional nonsingular Gaussian density. Singular PSD covariance describes a distribution confined to a lower-dimensional affine subspace. Key engineering invariants: all probabilities are valid and normalized; PDF units match the integration measure; covariance is symmetric PSD; Gaussian density evaluation avoids unnecessary inversion; nonfinite inputs and singular cases are explicit; sampling tests use statistical tolerances rather than exact equality.
