solve z=inverse(L)(x-mu); then Mahalanobis squared distance is z transpose z. A singular covariance is supported on a lower-dimensional affine subspace. Rebuild the numerical witness. Six figures
F10-1. Ordered outcomes and the exact two-dice sum PMF. The supplied lesson already derives this example; the figure is a visual check of the 36 ordered pairs. PMF numerators sum to 36 and P(S=7)=1/6.
F10-2. Zero covariance need not mean independence. For standard normal X, Cov(X,X squared)=0 by symmetry although X and X squared are dependent. Sample covariance is a finite-run witness.
F10-3. Uniform area sampling requires a square-root radial transform. The theoretical mean radius is 2/3 for uniform area in the unit disk and 1/2 for uniform radius; plotted sample means are finite-run illustrations.
F10-4. Monte Carlo random error and a fixed bias floor. For the stated integral, unbiased RMSE falls with sample count while the biased estimator retains its offset.
F10-5. A matched importance proposal can make contributions constant. For the stated nonnegative integrand and support, the matched proposal gives constant contributions; uniform-proposal variance is 4/45. This does not generalize to arbitrary signed integrands.
F10-6. A full-period toy LCG can still have a simple low-bit pattern. For m=16, a=5, c=1, all 16 states are visited but the least-significant bit alternates. Full period does not imply good multidimensional quality. The keyed-input sketch indicates deterministic indexing only: a different key does not establish statistical independence or collision freedom. Numerical reliability figures and their explanations
N10-7 · Summation is an algorithm, not just a plus sign — Exact real sum is 10000. The three-term counterexample shows why Kahan is not an exact-arithmetic guarantee. Strict IEEE-style evaluation is assumed; reassociation can invalidate compensation. N10-8 · More polynomial degree does not guarantee a better picture — Both interpolants match every node. Their behaviour between nodes differs. Chebyshev extrema reduce this example’s endpoint oscillation; this comparison is not a universal interpolation error bound. N10-9 · Bézier and Hermite can tell the same curve story — Use Hermite tangents 3(P1−P0) and 3(P3−P2) for this cubic Bézier curve. The control polygon bounds the curve through nonnegative weights summing to one; inner control points need not lie on the curve. N10-10 · A root solver needs both progress and a safety argument — The error comparison uses cos(x)−x with specified starting values. Bisection has a shrinking bracket; Newton and secant need additional hypotheses. The plotting floor is explicitly shown rather than interpreted as continuing convergence. N10-11 · Arbitrary sample counts need full-domain support — Left: choosing the first five of nine equal cells and averaging equally gives E[y] = 0.3, while the uniform-square value is 0.5. Right: one point per marginal bin is a midpoint illustration; randomized LHS jitters and permutes appropriately, and is not full multidimensional stratification. N10-12 · Algebraically equal formulas can have unequal numerical error — The reference uses 90-digit Decimal arithmetic and compares binary64 formulas for b from 100 to 10¹⁶. This bounded example illustrates cancellation, not a complete robust quadratic solver.

This companion appears in Volume 1, The Foundations Bible — Volume I: From Bits to Computation, C++, Memory and Systems: Basis coordinates and dimension — Basis coordinates and dimension Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: Phase6 · Latest development: Phase7 Definition and mechanism Phase 7 stores basis images as matrix columns and derives coordinate conversion <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mo stretchy="false">[</mo> <mi>v</mi> <msub> <mo stretchy="false">]</mo> <mi>C</mi> </msub> <mo>=</mo> <msup> <mi>C</mi> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"> <mo>−</mo> <mn>1</mn> </mrow> </msup> <mi>B</mi> <mo stretchy="false">[</mo> <mi>v</mi> <msub> <mo stretchy="false">]</mo> <mi>B</mi> </msub> </math>. The endpoint bases and whether motion is active or passive determine the product; row-major storage does not. Reconstruction and active/passive example. A basis is an ordered independent spanning set. Independence makes coordinates unique; spanning makes every vector reachable. Dimension counts basis elements over the chosen field, not stored components or bytes. A basis change alters coordinates without necessarily moving the physical vector. <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mn>3</mn> <mo>,</mo> <mn>2</mn> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> <mo>=</mo> <mn>1</mn> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mn>1</mn> <mo>,</mo> <mn>0</mn> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> <mo>+</mo> <mn>2</mn> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mn>1</mn> <mo>,</mo> <mn>1</mn> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </math>, so its slanted-basis coordinates are <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mn>1</mn> <mo>,</mo> <mn>2</mn> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </math>. A plane inside three-dimensional coordinates still has dimension two. Prerequisites
Vector spaces subspaces and span — Reachability and closure establish the spanning and independence questions.

Covectors linear functionals and normal transforms — Builds on this mechanism in the connected geometry story. Linear systems and fundamental subspaces — Extends this foundation into linear-systems and decomposition analysis. Spline bases and curve evaluation Additive energy and approximate structure Exceptional projections and dimension ## Recall and next depth
Separate passive coordinate change from active transformation and explain near-dependent basis sensitivity. Full production proofs, target-specific integration and learner mastery require further evidence. Appendix.title: Cross-volume companion reference
Appendix.Content:
This companion appears in Volume 2, The Foundations Bible — Volume II: Numerical Methods, Probability, Geometry and Camera Systems: Stable probability normalization and log-sum-exp — Stable probability normalization and log-sum-exp Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: Phase 10 · Latest development: Phase 10 Definition and mechanism To normalize nonnegative weights, divide each by their sum; direct summation can overflow even when the normalized probabilities are representable. Scale by the largest weight before summing. For log weights <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <msub> <mi>a</mi> <mi>i</mi> </msub> </math>, compute <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>m</mi> <mo>+</mo> <mi>log</mi> <mo data-mjx-texclass="NONE">⁡</mo> <munder> <mo data-mjx-texclass="OP">∑</mo> <mi>i</mi> </munder> <msup> <mi>e</mi> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"> <msub> <mi>a</mi> <mi>i</mi> </msub> <mo>−</mo> <mi>m</mi> </mrow> </msup> </math>, where <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>m</mi> <mo>=</mo> <munder> <mo data-mjx-texclass="OP" movablelimits="true">max</mo> <mi>i</mi> </munder> <msub> <mi>a</mi> <mi>i</mi> </msub> </math>. Subtracting the maximum prevents exponential overflow, and the result can be used to form softmax probabilities. This assumes at least one finite, valid weight and requires an explicit policy for all-zero, negative, NaN, or infinite inputs. Underflow of very small normalized probabilities is a separate concern from overflow; do not silently equate zero after underflow with mathematically impossible. For log weights <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mn>1000</mn> <mo>,</mo> <mn>1001</mn> <mo>,</mo> <mn>1000</mn> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </math>, subtracting <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mn>1001</mn> </math> keeps exponentials bounded while leaving the normalized probabilities unchanged. This companion appears in Volume 1, The Foundations Bible — Volume I: From Bits to Computation, C++, Memory and Systems: Jacobians, pushforwards, and pullbacks — Jacobians, pushforwards, and pullbacks Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: Phase 9 · Latest development: Phase 9 Definition and mechanism The Jacobian is the matrix of first derivatives of a vector-valued function. It maps a small input displacement to a first-order output displacement, a forward sensitivity often called a pushforward or Jacobian-vector product. Gradients transform in the reverse direction by the transpose Jacobian, the pullback used in reverse-mode differentiation. These operations differ because vectors and covectors have different transformation rules. Jacobians compose by matrix multiplication and their determinants describe local volume changes. A Jacobian is local: it does not replace a nonlinear transformation globally. At singular points it can lose rank or become ill-conditioned, affecting inverse sensitivity, uncertainty propagation, and optimizer steps. State coordinate ordering and column-vector conventions before interpreting signs or multiplication order. Prerequisites
Derivative as a local linear map Matrix multiplication and composition order Probability density and change of measure

Appendix.Content:
This companion appears in Volume 2, The Foundations Bible — Volume II: Numerical Methods, Probability, Geometry and Camera Systems: Cubic Hermite interpolation — Cubic Hermite interpolation Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: Phase 10 · Latest development: Phase 10 Definition and mechanism A cubic Hermite segment is determined by endpoint values and endpoint tangent data. With normalized <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>t</mi> <mo>∈</mo> <mo stretchy="false">[</mo> <mn>0</mn> <mo>,</mo> <mn>1</mn> <mo stretchy="false">]</mo> </math>, its four basis polynomials blend the two endpoint positions and two tangents. Tangents are derivatives with respect to the parameter, so physical-time derivatives must be scaled by segment duration: a velocity in units per second is not interchangeable with a tangent per normalized parameter. Hermite curves are useful when a camera path or animation must pass through known positions while exposing direct control over its entry and exit directions. The endpoint constraints determine one cubic polynomial; continuity between adjacent segments still requires compatible endpoint tangents. Prerequisites
Interpolation versus approximation Spline bases and curve evaluation

No downstream concept node is added in this stage.

Appendix.title: Cross-volume companion reference
Appendix.Content:
This companion appears in Volume 2, The Foundations Bible — Volume II: Numerical Methods, Probability, Geometry and Camera Systems: Bézier curves and De Casteljau evaluation — Bézier curves and De Casteljau evaluation Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: Phase 10 · Latest development: Phase 10 Definition and mechanism A Bézier curve blends control points with Bernstein basis weights. The weights are nonnegative and sum to one on <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mo stretchy="false">[</mo> <mn>0</mn> <mo>,</mo> <mn>1</mn> <mo stretchy="false">]</mo> </math>, so the curve remains in the control points’ convex hull and reaches its first and last control points at the endpoints. De Casteljau’s repeated linear interpolation evaluates the curve using numerically straightforward convex combinations; the intermediate levels also reveal subdivision geometry. A cubic Bézier’s endpoint tangents depend on its first and last control-polygon edges, so moving a handle changes direction and scale. The convex-hull guarantee applies to the curve parameter interval; extrapolation outside it loses that containment property. Subdivide the curve before tessellation when screen-space curvature changes rapidly; parameter steps alone do not guarantee uniform pixel error. Prerequisites
Interpolation versus approximation Spline bases and curve evaluation
Used by Full teaching explanation
Reconstructing values and curves between samples
Source coverage Supplied lesson parts: 983. Future keywords Bernstein basis, convex hull property, curve subdivision. Open Bézier curves and De Casteljau evaluation in Volume 2

Appendix.title: Cross-volume companion reference
Appendix.Content:
This companion appears in Volume 2, The Visual Computing Bible — Volume II: Computational Geometry, Vision, Reconstruction and XR: Optical flow and time to contact — Optical flow and time to contact Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: University courses · Latest development: University courses Definition and mechanism Optical flow is the apparent 2D motion of image features between frames. Under brightness constancy, a tracked point keeps approximately the same intensity as it moves, yielding the constraint <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <msub> <mi>I</mi> <mi>x</mi> </msub> <mi>u</mi> <mo>+</mo> <msub> <mi>I</mi> <mi>y</mi> </msub> <mi>v</mi> <mo>+</mo> <msub> <mi>I</mi> <mi>t</mi> </msub> <mo>=</mo> <mn>0</mn> </math>, where spatial derivatives <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <msub> <mi>I</mi> <mi>x</mi> </msub> <mo>,</mo> <msub> <mi>I</mi> <mi>y</mi> </msub> </math> and temporal derivative <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <msub> <mi>I</mi> <mi>t</mi> </msub> </math> are measured from the image and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mi>u</mi> <mo>,</mo> <mi>v</mi> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </math> is image velocity. One equation cannot determine two unknown components at a single pixel, so algorithms add neighborhood smoothness, feature tracking, or multiple scales. Flow can reveal camera motion, object motion, and looming. For an object approaching at speed <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>V</mi> </math>, its image size grows at a rate related to depth; the ratio of size to its time derivative estimates time to contact without separately knowing absolute scale under simplifying assumptions. Texture, occlusion, and illumination changes violate brightness constancy. Prerequisites
Spatiotemporal sampling and retinal motion Convolution and filter footprints
Used by

This companion appears in Volume 2, The Foundations Bible — Volume II: Numerical Methods, Probability, Geometry and Camera Systems: Surface tangents normals and bitangents — Surface tangents normals and bitangents Curriculum depth: Introduced · First seen: Phase6 · Latest development: Phase6 Definition and mechanism Tangents span local surface movement; normals measure perpendicularity; bitangents supply the second tangent axis. Texture derivatives carry physical stretch. Cleaned TBN frames need normalization, degeneracy checks and a mirrored-UV sign convention. Panel texture derivatives are <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mn>4</mn> <mo>,</mo> <mn>0</mn> <mo>,</mo> <mn>0</mn> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mn>0</mn> <mo>,</mo> <mn>3</mn> <mo>,</mo> <mn>0</mn> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </math> before normalization. A collapsed UV determinant cannot uniquely determine texture directions. Prerequisites
Cross products and oriented area — Oriented area supplies face normals, frame signs and geometric determinants. Unit directions and safe normalization — Validated finite unit directions establish the preconditions for simplified geometry formulas. Projection rejection and scalar components — Removing an unwanted component creates residuals, tangent axes and mirror decompositions.
Used by
Orthonormal frames and Gram-Schmidt — Builds on this mechanism in the connected geometry story.
Recall and next depth Derive the edge/UV equations and retain the handedness sign while orthogonalizing. Full production proofs, target-specific integration and learner mastery require further evidence. Appendix.title: Cross-volume companion reference
Appendix.Content:
This companion appears in Volume 2, The Visual Computing Bible — Volume II: Computational Geometry, Vision, Reconstruction and XR: Triangle rasterization and coverage tests — Triangle rasterization and coverage tests Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: University courses · Latest development: University courses Definition and mechanism Rasterization converts triangle geometry into a finite set of image samples. A pixel’s ideal coverage is the area fraction inside the triangle; a center test approximates this integral with one binary answer and therefore creates jagged edges. A directed edge defines an inside half-plane, so three signed edge tests classify a point against a triangle. A consistent tie rule assigns samples exactly on shared edges to one triangle, preventing cracks and double coverage. Supersampling tests several locations per pixel and averages their coverage, trading cost for a better area estimate. Hardware often checks candidate samples in parallel within a bounding box, then rejects or accepts coarse blocks that are wholly outside or inside. Triangle coverage is also the basis for interpolating depth, color, normals, and texture coordinates. Prerequisites
Barycentric coordinates and interpolation Sampling aliasing and reconstruction
Used by
Worlds, Images and Inference Depth buffering and visibility order Homogeneous clipping and perspective interpolation ## Full teaching explanation
A scene description becomes an image · Rasterization, coverage, and depth. Open Triangle rasterization and coverage tests in Volume 2

Appendix.title: Cross-volume companion reference
Appendix.Content:
This companion appears in Volume 1, The Foundations Bible — Volume I: From Bits to Computation, C++, Memory and Systems: Prefix scan and stream compaction — Prefix scan and stream compaction A prefix scan turns local counts into globally consistent offsets. For an exclusive sum scan of input <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>x</mi> </math>, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block"> <msub> <mi>y</mi> <mn>0</mn> </msub> <mo>=</mo> <mn>0</mn> <mo>,</mo> <mstyle scriptlevel="0"> <mspace width="2em" /> </mstyle> <msub> <mi>y</mi> <mi>i</mi> </msub> <mo>=</mo> <munderover> <mo data-mjx-texclass="OP">∑</mo> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"> <mi>j</mi> <mo>=</mo> <mn>0</mn> </mrow> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"> <mi>i</mi> <mo>−</mo> <mn>1</mn> </mrow> </munderover> <msub> <mi>x</mi> <mi>j</mi> </msub> <mo>.</mo> </math> If each element says how many output records it will emit, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <msub> <mi>y</mi> <mi>i</mi> </msub> </math> is the first output slot owned by element <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>i</mi> </math>. This converts a race-prone global append into deterministic non-overlapping regions. For Boolean compaction, let predicate <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <msub> <mi>b</mi> <mi>i</mi> </msub> <mo>∈</mo> <mo fence="false" stretchy="false">{</mo> <mn>0</mn> <mo>,</mo> <mn>1</mn> <mo fence="false" stretchy="false">}</mo> </math>. Scan <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>b</mi> </math> to obtain offsets. Every active element with <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <msub> <mi>b</mi> <mi>i</mi> </msub> <mo>=</mo> <mn>1</mn> </math> writes itself to output[scan[i]]. The final output count is scan[n-1] + b[n-1]. Parallel structure The naive parallel scan that repeatedly doubles an offset performs <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>O</mi> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mi>n</mi> <mi>log</mi> <mo data-mjx-texclass="NONE">⁡</mo> <mi>n</mi> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </math> work. A work-efficient tree scan performs an up-sweep/reduction followed by a down-sweep and uses <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>O</mi> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mi>n</mi> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </math> work with <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>O</mi> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mi>log</mi> <mo data-mjx-texclass="NONE">⁡</mo> <mi>n</mi> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </math> depth. On a GPU, a practical large-array scan normally has several levels:
scan each workgroup block into local output; record each block total; scan the block totals; add each scanned block offset back into that block’s local results.
Every phase has a dependency. Dispatching all phases without establishing visibility/order is not a valid scan merely because each shader is individually correct. Shared-memory bank conflicts and subgroup width affect performance, while workgroup barriers only synchronize participating invocations in that workgroup. Stream compaction as an allocation proof Compaction is useful beyond filtering visible objects. It appears in GPU-driven draw generation, BVH construction, particle survival, tiled light lists, Gaussian tile duplication and sparse work queues. The scan proves that each surviving producer owns a distinct range before any scatter writes occur. Evidence boundary The current repository has CPU-side scan/compaction reasoning in the canonical volumes but does not yet claim a native Vulkan/Metal scan kernel benchmark. The next hardware proof should compare a scalar CPU oracle, a workgroup implementation, multi-workgroup hierarchy, adversarial non-power-of-two sizes, and captured GPU timing. Primary background: NVIDIA GPU Gems 3, Chapter 39, “Parallel Prefix Sum (Scan) with CUDA.” Teach and reconstruct: Continuous Notes/Computing Foundations - From Bits to C++ and Systems APIs#Scan turns local counts into nonoverlapping output regions. Related: GPU workgroups and synchronization, BVH build traversal and workload selection.. Open Prefix scan and stream compaction in Volume 1

This companion appears in Volume 2, The Foundations Bible — Volume II: Numerical Methods, Probability, Geometry and Camera Systems: Unit directions and safe normalization — Unit directions and safe normalization Curriculum depth: Introduced · First seen: Phase6 · Latest development: Phase6 Definition and mechanism A unit direction is finite, nonzero input scaled to approximate length one. Scale by the largest absolute component before measuring to avoid unnecessary squared overflow or underflow. Zero has no direction; application noise thresholds are distinct from numerical existence. For finite nonzero input, scaled squared length lies between <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mn>1</mn> </math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mn>3</mn> </math>. A vector of huge components can have a computable unit direction even when its original length does not fit. Prerequisites
Norms lengths and induced distances — Lengths and their domains are needed before unit directions or angular measurements. Robust norm and intermediate range — Range-safe scaling avoids losing a valid direction to unnecessary squared intermediates.
Used by
Robust vector angles — Builds on this mechanism in the connected geometry story. Surface tangents normals and bitangents — Builds on this mechanism in the connected geometry story. Reflection refraction and shading directions — Builds on this mechanism in the connected geometry story. Coordinate-space types and validated invariants — Builds on this mechanism in the connected geometry story. Axial depth and Euclidean range Omnidirectional camera projections Screen-space ray generation and mouse picking ## Recall and next depth
Reconstruct the bounds and distinguish rejection, a caller fallback, and a validated wrapper. Full production proofs, target-specific integration and learner mastery require further evidence. Appendix.title: Cross-volume companion reference
Appendix.Content:
This companion appears in Volume 2, The Visual Computing Bible — Volume II: Computational Geometry, Vision, Reconstruction and XR: Manifold polygon meshes and boundary structure — Manifold polygon meshes and boundary structure Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: University courses · Latest development: University courses Definition and mechanism A polygon mesh is a combinatorial surface made of vertices, edges, and faces plus an embedding that assigns each vertex a position. Manifoldness is a local connectivity condition: an interior edge belongs to two faces, and the faces around each interior vertex form one cycle or fan. At a boundary, an edge belongs to one face and the vertex neighborhood forms one open chain; each boundary component closes into a loop. A bow-tie vertex with two disconnected fans is nonmanifold even if every face is an ordinary triangle. These conditions let algorithms define an unambiguous local tangent neighborhood, traversal, and surface orientation. Connectivity validity does not guarantee good geometry: valid topology can still self-intersect, collapse to a point, or contain poor skinny triangles. Keep topological and geometric quality checks separate. Prerequisites
Coordinate frames and change of basis
Used by
Worlds, Images and Inference Half-edge mesh connectivity Quadric error mesh simplification Bounding volume hierarchies Collision barriers and continuous detection Local rigidity and mesh orientation fields ## Full teaching explanation
Surfaces, patches, topology, and parameterization · Meshes, connectivity, and geometry processing · Surface descriptions and Gaussian images. Open Manifold polygon meshes and boundary structure in Volume 2

This companion appears in Volume 1, The Foundations Bible — Volume I: From Bits to Computation, C++, Memory and Systems: Matrix storage indexing and strides — Matrix storage indexing and strides Curriculum depth: Introduced · First seen: Phase7 · Latest development: Phase7 Definition and mechanism Matrix row/column semantics are independent of physical row-major or column-major storage. A strided view uses explicit row and column strides, shape, backing extent, and borrow lifetime. Separate named scalar members are not an array eligible for pointer indexing. Reconstruction cue: For row-major strides row=8 and column=1, element (2,3) has scalar offset 19. Prerequisites
